title: Dalton Knecht Emerges as Likely Lakers Roster Casualty
description: The Los Angeles Lakers may be gearing up to cut former first-round pick Dalton Knecht, according to a new report, as they shape the roster. The post Dalton Knecht Emerges as Likely Lakers Roster Casualty appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Lakers may be gearing up to cut former first-round pick Dalton Knecht, according to a new report, as they shape the roster.

The Lakers currently have 16 players on the roster, and by the time the season rolls around, that number will need to be 15.

On the bright side for the Lakers, they have depth and a good roster-building choice, but the decision will be tricky.

Among the players on the chopping block is Knecht, who is expected to be the odd man out according to a report from Khobi Price of the California Post.

"Not a good sign for Knecht, whom multiple rival executives expect to be the odd man out as the Lakers look to trim their roster from 16 players on standard NBA deals to the league maximum of 15," Price wrote in his report.

Knecht was taken with the No. 17 overall pick back in the 2024 NBA Draft. However, midway through his rookie year, he was traded to the Hornets for center Mark Williams, but the trade was ultimately canceled.

Williams stayed with the Hornets, and Knecht returned to the Lakers, leading to an awkward reintegration period.

He struggled since then to look like the promising player that he once was.

Still, JJ Redick sees a player who is trying hard and wants to make the team and get minutes.

"First of all, he's been a pro," Redick said. "He's been in the gym. Like he has since Day 1, he has worked his butt off all offseason. And he's had a good three days of practice. So I don't think his approach changes. I know he's hungry to play and hungry to earn a spot in the rotation."

Knecht shot 37.6% from deep his rookie year, then 34.2% the following season. As a shooter, he needs to start shooting more efficiently.

If he can find his confidence and start creating offense again, Knecht could beat the odds and stay with the team.

He has a role on the wings, but he will need to take it.

title: ‘Stop throwing a pity party’: Brady Quinn rips Deshaun Watson for acting like a victim

fullText:
The Cleveland Browns defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers 27-24 on Thursday night, improving the team to 3-1 on the season. The Browns' early-season success has been one of the biggest surprises in the NFL this year, and it is in large part thanks to the massively improved play from veteran quarterback Deshaun Watson.

The FOX Sports Radio morning show, 2 Pros and a Cup of Joe, hosted by Brady Quinn, LaVar Arrington, and Jonas Knox, discussed the story surrounding the Browns on Friday morning.

"Credit due, hat off to (head coach Todd Monken)," Arrington said. "He has the Cleveland Browns at 3-1 after a divisional opponent in the Pittsburgh Steelers, who were coming off of a big victory over the Cincinnati Bengals. So give them credit. But I think this is honestly, potentially, this is more of an indictment on the Pittsburgh Steelers than it is a feel-good story for the Cleveland Browns.

“STOP throwing a pity party for what’s happened in the past for yourself. You won a game; make it about everyone besides YOU because, quite frankly, you’re on a really good team!”

– @Brady_Quinn on the Deshaun Watson PR spin. pic.twitter.com/Wab9BaPcmy

— FOX Sports Radio (@FoxSportsRadio) October 2, 2026

"I don't understand this need for a, well, feel-good story," Knox said. "I don't get it. What were the struggles? Let's just like break down the struggles. The struggles were: you had a fetish with the handhouse, and you weren't available. And then when you were available to play after suspension, you were injured. And then when you weren't injured, you were bad."

Quinn went on to make it clear that while he's happy for Browns' fans, he doesn't see why Deshaun Watson is throwing a "pity party" for himself.

"I feel good for the Cleveland fans. Yes. I feel good for a lot of those players," Quinn said. "I'm not sure what PR spin they're trying to put on or revisionist history they're trying to make. Anything that he endured in the past, he brought on himself. I mean, there's, there's not one part of the adversity he faced that he should have been solely responsible for.

"So like, here's the unfortunate part is we have— we're going to keep talking about this because they're going to keep bringing it up and we're going to have to keep addressing it, acknowledging it. Like, dude, stop throwing a pity party. For what's happened in the past for yourself. All right, you won a game, make it about the team, make it about everyone besides you, because quite frankly, you're on a really good team and it is about everyone besides you.

"Like, you're the quarterback, all right? This isn't Lamar Jackson in college running around carrying Louisville or at times carrying Baltimore. Like, you are there because— and you're being successful because of the help you have around you. So I just, I hope he stops with keep trying to get people to feel bad for him."

The Browns and Watson will next face the New York Jets.

The biography explores the influence of the late owner of the Buffalo Bills across 50 years in the NFL, as well as his business ventures, philanthropy, and service in World War II.

Tranter said that fans of the Bills will be fans of his book.

"It's the history of the team through his eyes, so I think they'll really like that," Tranter said. "I think they'll learn things about him that people don't know, like his military history; he was a naval guy for World War II, he spent five years in the Navy, and there's some great stories about him in the Navy, so I think they'll appreciate all that."

title: Nine scandals that rocked the sporting world
description: Manchester City are far from the first. The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of other sports stars to break the rules.
fullText:
Manchester City being found guilty of fuelling an era of glittering Premier League success via a network of sponsorship deals, found by an independent commision to be a "sham", has shaken the world of sport.

The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of others to cheat.

BBC Sport looks back on nine more sporting scandals, stretching back more than a century.

Cancer survivor. Cycling legend. American hero. Cheat.

Lance Armstrong had spent years vehemently and aggressively insisting that he had won all seven of his Tour de France titles between 1999 and 2005 without the help of performance-enhancing drugs.

His story was remarkable. Aged 25, Armstrong had been diagnosed with testicular cancer, with doctors warning he was likely to die given the disease had spread to other parts of his body.

He not only survived, but returned to dominate top-level cycling. His Livestrong Foundation was wildly successful, selling millions of yellow wristbands to raise money to support fellow cancer sufferers.

However, as the evidence and former team-mates allegations against him stacked up, Armstrong was stripped of his Tour de France titles.

Armstong eventually confessed to cheating in a blockbuster interview with talk show host Oprah Winfrey.

"I made those decisions, they were my mistake and I'm here to say sorry," he said, adding that the culture in professional cycling made using drugs non-negotiable.

Armstrong says sorry for doping

Hansie Cronje was the golden boy of South African sport.

Good looking and charming, he led the nation's cricket team with style and authority.

President Nelson Mandela singled out Cronje in 1996 for the "excellent manner" in which he captained the Proteas.

However, Cronje's love of money, combined with a fast-growing betting industry and the organised crime it attracted, proved his downfall.

Cronje entertained the offers of match-fixers, calling team meetings to discuss the possibility of throwing matches and sharing thousands of dollars in inducements.

Most infamously, Cronje contrived to lose a rain-affected Test against England in 2000.

With South Africa still in the midst of their first innings on the final day, Cronje convinced England counterpart Nasser Hussein that in the interest of sporting entertainment each side should forfeit an innings, producing a sudden run-chase and giving England a shot at victory.

Cronje was praised for his Corinthian spirit. In reality, he had been motivated by a bribe of £5,000 to ensure the match did not end in a draw.

Cronje was undone when an Indian police wiretap of a bookmaker caught him in discussions about fixing matches.

Cronje confessed in early 2000, was banned from cricket for life and died in a plane crash two years later at the age of 32.

Hansie Cronje, match-fixing and plane crash that left a complex legacy

There was something particular about turn 17 of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

In 2008, before the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix was held at the circuit, Renault driver Nelson Piquet Jr knew it did not have any overhead cranes to lift a damaged car from the track. There were no side entrances to allow a stranded driver to be pushed out of danger's way by marshalls either.

On lap 14 Piquet found himself in exactly in that unfortunate position. And, despite his initial claim that he had made a "simple mistake", the Brazilian had put himself there deliberately.

When Renault dropped him in 2009, Piquet Jr revealed that he steered himself into a concrete wall to crash his car. The safety car was deployed as officials cleared debris off the track.

Crucially, Piquet Jr's team-mate Fernando Alonso was the only frontrunner to have stopped for fuel and new tyres at the point of the crash.

As Alonso's rivals went into the pits, the Spaniard, benefitting from the reduced gaps caused by the safety car, moved up the field and went on to win the race.

While Alonso was cleared of any wrongdoing or knowledge of the plot, Renault team principal Flavio Briatore and chief technical officer Pat Symonds were banned from F1 for several years.

Still in F1 10 years after 'crashgate'

Frank Lampard wheeled away in celebration after his well-hit shot from the edge of the penalty area beat Kevin Miller in the Crystal Palace goal in the 65th minute of a Monday evening Premier League game in November 1997.

As he was mobbed by team-mates, Upton Park was plunged into darkness.

The following month similar happened at Selhurst Park. Thirteen seconds into the second half - with Wimbledon and Arsenal goalless - the lights went off. The Christmas lights in nearby Croydon were raised as a possible cause.

The actual cause was more sinister.

An Asian betting syndicate had pulled the plug, using a remote control circuit breaker, to get each match abandoned at a scoreline which would maximise their profits.

The gang were foiled in their attempts to pull the deception for a third time. They had bribed a security guard at Charlton Athletic to allow them to plant a device at The Valley before Liverpool's visit in February.

However, a suspicious member of staff at the club tipped off police.

Four men were given sentences of between 18 months and four years for their involvement.

Four jailed for floodlight plot

No expense was spared for the Winter Olympics in Sochi in 2014.

With a budget of $50bn (£38bn) - more than 25 times Vancouver's 2010 Winter Olympics spend - organisers created two entirely new resorts, bristling with security and military personnel.

But building facilities from scratch also gave the Russian hosts a chance to design an elaborate way around anti-doping measures.

A secret tunnel allowed a Russian secret service agent, disguised as a sewer engineer, to swap out his compatriots' urine samples, which contained traces of banned substances.

A special method had been developed to remove the tamperproof lids of sample bottles, which were then refilled with 'clean' urine that had been frozen before Russian athletes began doping programmes.

Forty-three Russian athletes were banned for life, 28 of whom successfully appealed against the full extent of their punishment.

Russia was banned from competing at the following Winter Olympics in South Korea, although athletes who could demonstrate their clean record were permitted to compete under a neutral flag.

Russia banned from 2018 Winter Olympics

A camera crew caught the aftermath of the attack on Nancy Kerrigan in January 1994.

The 24-year-old figure skater was captured clutching her leg and repeatedly wailing "why?".

Kerrigan had been training at a rink in Detroit before the American national championships. As she stepped off the ice, a man rushed towards her and struck her on the leg with a telescopic baton.

Kerrigan's 'why' was soon answered.

The bodyguard and ex-husband of Kerrigan's rival Tonya Harding had hired a man to break Kerrigan's leg. They hoped to rule her out of the forthcoming Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, boosting Harding's chances.

It didn't work. Kerrigan recovered from heavy bruising in time to make the USA team, alongside Harding.

Amid a media frenzy, Harding, struggling with a broken lace on her boot, finished eighth in the Olympic final.

The competition broke viewing records in the US.

Harding was banned for life from the sport after admitting attempting to conceal the identity of Kerrigan's assailant after the attack.

Harding's ex-husband Jeff Gillooly, the attacker he hired and a getaway driver all spent time in prison for their part in the crime.

When Olympic figure skating met whodunnit

The headline written in the Chicago Daily News summed up the disbelief of a city, a nation and a sport when it emerged that superstar Joe Jackson and seven of his Chicago White Sox team-mates had apparently taken bribes to lose the 1919 World Series, baseball's biggest game.

First baseman Chick Gandil was the ringleader, while star pitcher Eddie Cicotte was the key figure.

A fee of $100,000 - worth about $1.6m today - was agreed with the head of a betting syndicate, with the money to be shared among the eight conspirators.

Cicotte's pitch, deliberately hitting Maurice Rath on the back, was a sign to his team-mates, and gamblers in the know, that the fix was on.

After the White Sox lost the series 5-3 to the Cincinnati Reds, the White Sox's suspicious owner Charles Comiskey sent word that the players needed to collect their pay cheques from him in person.

None of the eight fixers did. They left the stadium without their money. Rumours spread, followed by an investigation, and soon the players were in the dock.

Although a criminal court failed to convict the players, they were banned from Major League Baseball for life.

Jackson insisted until his death in 1951 that he was not involved and that, despite receiving $5,000, he had been deceived into signing a confession.

The data revolutionary who exposed baseball's big fix

At half-time in their first match at the 2000 Paralympics the coach of Spain's intellectual disability basketball team told them to stop scoring so quickly and let their opponents shoot more.

He knew the vast majority of the team were there under false pretences.

Of the 12 players in the squad, 10 had no intellectual impairment at all, but were keen amateur players who had been recruited months before the Sydney Games to supplement the team.

Spain, perhaps unsurprisingly, won gold convincingly, beating Russia 87-63 in the final.

The scam unravelled because one of the ringers was also a journalist.

Realising he was in the midst of an incredible scoop, Carlos Ribagorda played in Sydney and then published an article detailing the scandal on his return.

The team were stripped of their medals and the incident led to a total ban on athletes with an intellectual disability from the 2004 and 2008 Paralympics, destroying the careers of thousands of sportspeople around the world.

Fake Paralympians boss: 'I didn't know about cheating'

When public prosecutors tapped telephone calls at Italian football giants Juventus in 2004, they were hunting for evidence of doping.

What they believed they found was corruption on a far more systematic scale.

They thought they had evidence of Juve general manager Luciano Moggi pressurising referee officials to favour certain clubs, including his own. Moggi denied the claims.

However, Juve, AC Milan, Fiorentina, Lazio and Reggina were all implicated in influencing referees.

All were given points deductions, but only Juventus ultimately dropped into the second tier of Italian football.

There was a split in the club's superstar squad.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Patrick Vieira joined rivals Inter Milan for a combined £23m, Fabio Cannavaro and Emerson went to Real Madrid for £13.7m, Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta joined Barcelona for £13m, and Adrian Mutu went to Fiorentina for £5.5m.

But other key players – notably Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro del Piero, Giorgio Chiellini, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet – remained with Juve in Serie B.

Despite beginning the season with a nine-point penalty and an opening-day draw with minnows Rimini, Juventus were promoted at the first attempt.

The club still lay claim to the 2004–05 and 2005–06 titles that were stripped from them, counting 38 rather than the official 36.

title: Senator appears to misstate sports teams in attempt to link Jack Smith to Fani Willis

fullText:
Apparent confusion over team names derailed a line of questioning as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) grilled former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday about his attendance at a basketball game, suggesting the prosecutor may have coordinated with others bringing charges about President Trump.

The exchange would later prompt Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) to say the panel had been "witness to a narrative, a false narrative of accusing [Smith] of being at a game that you were nowhere near, and I suppose that was supposed to be in furtherance of some sort of conspiracy."

Schmitt asked Smith if he had traveled to Atlanta in 2024 to watch an Atlanta Hawks basketball game, alluding to the trip as a chance to meet Fani Willis, the top prosecutor in the city. Willis also brought charges against Trump.

Schmitt said he had texts referencing the game, though a board displaying the messages was only briefly shown by the senator's staff.

Schmitt seemed surprised when Smith said he did not recall going to Atlanta during that time period and also said he did not meet Willis. For his part, Smith seemed puzzled.

"I really don't think so. It's possible I flew through the Atlanta airport on the way to Florida, but I do not have a recollection of going to Atlanta. I definitely did not go to a Hawks game," Smith said.

The significance of the trip from Schmitt's perspective was that the February 2024 game he referenced was the day after Willis revealed she was in a relationship with one of her own staffers, sparking a firestorm of scrutiny around the already high-profile Fulton County election interference case.

"Let me just give you a little context. The day before Fani Willis came clean with her affair with the prosecutor, you know, the Atlanta prosecutor that was also trying to get Trump. The next day, were you in Atlanta?" Schmitt asked.

Smith said he had at one point attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland, as he wanted to watch Caitlin Clark play.

Schmitt's questioning ended with the lawmaker calling Smith a "villain" and "dirtbag."

Amid protests from Democrats, Schmitt initially refused to again show the text messages he displayed on the board, prompting some to say Smith deserved to see what he was being asked to respond to. Schmitt later relented.

The text messages show one prosecutor on Smith's team having booked a meeting room only to be told by another staffer that Smith is "already down here." The text messages he displayed don't reference any basketball team names or games, though Schmitt at one point told Smith, "I don't think you know that we have this stuff."

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who was next in line for questioning, posited that Schmitt may have confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes.

"Could it then be that University of Iowa is the Hawkeyes? … That might be the confusion over the names of the team," she said.

"That might be the confusion over the names of the team. But perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully."

Schmitt then snapped that Klobuchar was trying to "rehabilitate the witness."

After wrapping her questioning, Klobuchar criticized Schmitt for calling the prosecutor a "dirtbag."

"We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93 to 85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over 30 points, so it must have been a pretty good game. The game was, in fact, in Maryland, Mr. Smith," she said.

"And I would just say, for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology."

title: How much has ESPN changed since Stephen A. Smith joined the network?
description: T.Schneider/Depositphotos ESPN was already a major sports operation ESPN Inc. was already a large sports media operation when Stephen A. Smith joined in 2003 as an NBA Shootaround analyst. That year, the company also launched ESPN HD for high-definition television coverage.
fullText:
ESPN Inc. was already a large sports media operation when Stephen A. Smith joined in 2003 as an NBA Shootaround analyst. That year, the company also launched ESPN HD for high-definition television coverage.

Stephen A. Smith began at ESPN as an NBA studio analyst and later appeared on SportsCenter, ESPN News, First Take, and Pardon the Interruption. Those assignments gave him roles across several established programs.

Smith also hosted The Stephen A. Smith Show on ESPN Radio from 2005 through 2008. His early network work combined basketball analysis, general sports commentary, radio hosting, and recurring television appearances.

Stephen A. Smith received his own ESPN2 program in 2005 with Quite Frankly with Stephen A. Smith. The one-hour show featured sports news, commentary, and interviews before ending its run in 2007.

Quite Frankly gave Smith a dedicated television format before First Take became his signature ESPN role. His first tenure at the network ended in 2008, while his later return led to a larger morning presence.

Stephen A. Smith returned to ESPN programming in 2011 and joined First Take full-time in June 2012. The revised format featured Smith and Skip Bayless debating major sports topics at the desk.

First Take also introduced a new set, graphics, and format during that June relaunch. By September 2012, year-to-date viewership had risen 33%, while the third-quarter audience had increased 21% from the same period in 2011.

Stephen A. Smith became a central commentator on First Take as the program expanded its audience. By 2014, viewership among men ages 18 to 34 had increased for six consecutive years.

That same audience group grew 25% during 2014, while First Take became ESPN2's most-watched studio show. The figures established the debate program as a major part of ESPN's weekday schedule.

First Take expanded beyond linear television as digital viewing grew. In 2023, the program averaged 496,000 television viewers, setting its highest annual average at that point in the show's history.

First Take content also generated 250 million YouTube views during 2023, while its social accounts reached a combined 4.5 million followers. Those totals showed substantial consumption outside the television broadcast.

First Take set another annual audience record in 2025, averaging 517,000 viewers. The total increased 6% from 2024 and marked the program's most-watched calendar year through the end of 2025.

Other ESPN studio programs also grew that year. Get Up averaged 424,000 viewers, while NFL Live posted its strongest annual performance since 2016, showing that audience gains extended beyond First Take.

Stephen A. Smith signed a new multi-year ESPN agreement in March 2025 that keeps him with the company for at least five more years. The deal also covers appearances across additional ESPN programming.

Smith remains First Take's featured commentator and executive producer. He also co-executive produces the program through Mr. SAS Productions, alongside ESPN and Omaha Productions, which gives him responsibilities beyond appearing on camera.

ESPN expanded into subscription streaming with ESPN+ in April 2018. The paid service launched inside the ESPN App and added thousands of live events, original programming, and on-demand sports content.

That transition advanced on August 21, 2025, when ESPN launched a direct subscription service carrying its full network lineup. Fans gained access to those channels without needing a traditional television package.

ESPN's expanded direct subscription service launched an Unlimited plan at $29.99 per month. The package provided access to ESPN networks and services, covering about 47,000 live events at launch.

The enhanced ESPN App also introduced multiview options, integrated game statistics, fantasy features, and personalized SportsCenter content. Those additions combine live viewing, information, and account features into one digital platform.

Fun fact: Before becoming ESPN's loudest debate fixture, Stephen A. Smith attended college on a basketball scholarship and played for legendary coach Clarence "Big House" Gaines.

Juan Alejandro Bernal R/Deopsitphotos

ESPN added Monday Night Football to its cable schedule in 2006 after the franchise moved from ABC. The change placed one of the NFL's longest-running prime-time packages directly on ESPN each week.

The 2024 Monday Night Football season averaged 15 million viewers per game and reached 112 million people. Those figures show the continuing scale of NFL programming within ESPN's broader television and streaming business.

ESPN and Disney secured new 11-year NBA and WNBA media agreements. The NBA agreement began with the 2025 to 2026 season, while the WNBA agreement started with its 2026 season.

The agreements run through the 2035-2036 NBA season and the 2036 WNBA season. ABC remains the exclusive NBA Finals television home, while ESPN distributes basketball coverage across television and streaming platforms.

"I wouldn't be surprised," Clark predicts that overseas WNBA games next year offer added context on how her influence may extend beyond domestic competition as the league considers broader international opportunities.

ESPN has expanded from a cable-centered sports network into a business spanning television, streaming, digital products, and audio since Stephen A. Smith first joined the company as an NBA analyst in 2003.

Smith's career followed that broader shift from studio analyst to featured commentator and executive producer. ESPN also added direct subscriptions, richer digital tools, and expanded rights packages as sports viewing habits changed.

fullText:
Big-time college sports has moved halfway toward the federal bailout they crave. The rest of the journey is unlikely to happen soon.

The U.S. Senate passed the so-called "Protect College Sports Act" on Monday night, by a vote of 77-22. The bill now goes to the U.S. House of Representatives.

Earlier in the day, Pat Forde of SI.com cited an unnamed source who said that there is a "0.0 percent chance" the House will pass the bill before the midterm elections.

With the Democrats widely expected to seize control of the House in November, the question then becomes whether it will do any meaningful business before the next Congress convenes in January.

So there's still a long way to go before the NCAA and its members get the antitrust exemption and other benefits designed to stave off a catastrophe. Even as college football is more popular and profitable than ever.

There's chaos, they say. From whose perspective? The players, after years of being exploited by a system that denied them the opportunity to participate meaningfully in the value they generate, are sitting pretty. It's not chaotic for them; it's the free market in operation.

But the schools apparently can't be trusted to balance their budgets, which is bullshit. Every American business faces an ongoing challenge to adapt or fail. In lieu of expecting the administrators to come up with a better way to carve up the pie and/or to spend within their means, they want artificial restrictions on what the players can make.

That's not how it should be. And, despite the Senate vote, maybe it won't be.

fullText:
After the Protect College Sports Act passed a full Senate vote 77-23 on Monday, each of the power conference released a statement praising the advancement. The bipartisan legislation will now head to the U.S. House of Representatives.

The power conferences all voiced their support for the Protect College Sports Act as it went through the Senate. At first, only the Big 12 and ACC were on board, but the SEC and Big Ten announced their full support in late July to give the bill some momentum. The NCAA also supported it and released its statement shortly after passage.

From there, the bill advanced out of a markup and committee vote, as well as multiple procedural votes. After debate and votes on amendments Monday, the legislation passed the Senate. It will now head to the House, which is not due back in session until after the midterm elections.

"The bipartisan Senate passage of the Protect College Sports Act represents an important step toward establishing a clear and durable national framework for college athletics," the SEC said in its statement. "We look forward to working with members of the House of Representatives to advance legislation that protects student-athletes, provides consistent national standards for universities and conferences, supports women's and Olympic sports, and strengthens the long-term future of college athletics.

"The SEC and our 16 member universities will remain actively and constructively engaged as the legislative process continues, with the goal of achieving a national framework that provides stability, accountability, and clarity for college sports."

In its statement, the Big Ten credited the Senators who sponsored the bill. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) introduced it in late May, and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) joined as co-sponsors.

"We are pleased the Protect College Sports Act has passed the Senate, and are appreciative of the substantial work that has gone into the effort from the act's authors, sponsors, and supporters," the Big Ten's statement read. "We look forward to the next steps to passage as we continue to support the act as passed by the Senate."

Additionally, the Big 12 cited the importance of the Protect College Sports Act's advancement. The conference cited the need to "move beyond uncertainty" as the landscape continues to shift in the NIL and revenue-share eras.

"We are encouraged by the continued progress of the Protect College Sports Act and appreciate the bipartisan leadership of Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell, and others that has moved this effort forward," the Big 12's statement read. "The legislation provides a more stable national framework for college athletics, incorporates important transparency measures, and moves our industry closer to a sustainable model that supports student-athletes, institutions, conferences, and fans.

"The future of college sports depends on our ability to move beyond uncertainty and toward lasting solutions, and the Protect College Sports Act is an important step in that direction. We look forward to working with lawmakers as the process advances."

The Protect College Sports Act would grant the NCAA an antitrust exemption to limit athletes to one transfer without penalty, standardize the new five-year, age-based eligibility policy, increase the revenue-sharing cap to nearly $50, put more enforcement in place around the rev-share cap, create an agent registry with a maximum 5% fee and allow schools to pool together their media rights, among other things.

Three amendments were added to the Protect College Sports Act on Monday after the Senate voted on seven of them. One would increase the conference limit to 20 members, rather than the 19 members in the bill's initial text, and another would require schools to disclose foreign funding in college sports. The third would allow states to pass more health and safety requirements through statute and common law.

Up next for the Protect College Sports Act is the House of Representatives. However, the House moved to take two weeks out of its calendar and is not due back until November, after the midterm elections. Cruz has expressed optimism the House will return to vote on the legislation.

Should the bill advance out of the House, it would then head to President Donald Trump's desk. Trump has been a strong supporter of the legislation, and Cruz has suggested he sign it into law on ESPN's College GameDay.

title: How the Protect College Sports Act could affect Charlie Woods and college golf
description: A new Senate bill seeks to stabilize college sports amid NIL chaos, potentially impacting stars like Charlie Woods.
fullText:
TaylorMade's decision to sign Charlie Woods to an NIL deal looked significant when it was announced earlier this month. Now, with federal lawmakers moving closer to reshaping the entire college sports landscape, the agreement may look even more consequential.

The Protect College Sports Act cleared a major hurdle this week after passing the Senate and advancing to the House of Representatives, bringing college athletics a step closer to the most sweeping federal overhaul in years. Supporters say the legislation would bring stability to a system upended by unrestricted player movement, conference realignment and a rapidly evolving name, image and likeness marketplace.

In a 77-22 vote on Capitol Hill on Monday, Sept. 28, the years-long legislative proposal formally cleared its first major hurdle, with eight co-sponsors, headlined by the early work of Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.).

"The most important part of the bill is bringing order to chaos," Cruz told USA TODAY Sports. "College sports is the Wild West. There are essentially no rules. Litigation has struck down virtually all the rules, and as a result, you have athletes going into the transfer portal two, three, four times. You have athletes competing for seven or eight years. You have 27, 28-year-olds competing against 17-year-olds. You have pro players coming back and playing college sports, and every school is in a spending spiral where virtually every athletic department is losing millions of dollars. Many of them are losing tens of millions of dollars. It's unsustainable, and as a consequence, every week we see a different problem.

"Programs being canceled, we see women's sports being canceled. We see Olympic sports being canceled, and if Congress doesn't act within a few years, we will see hundreds of thousands of roster slots and scholarship positions going away, and that would be a tragedy. It would be a tragedy because every year right now we have roughly 500,000 college athletes in America."

For golf, the bill could have far-reaching implications.

When TaylorMade signed Woods, the son of 15-time major champion Tiger Woods, the move underscored how NIL opportunities have expanded beyond traditional revenue sports. Woods, who is committed to Florida State and entering his senior year of high school, became one of the most visible examples of a golfer leveraging his personal brand before arriving on a college campus.

At the time, the agreement signaled more than an equipment partnership. It reflected the growing value of elite amateur golfers as marketing assets. While top junior players have long received free clubs, balls and apparel from manufacturers, paid NIL agreements remain relatively rare in college golf. One Division I men's coach recently estimated that only a few dozen players currently have manufacturer deals that include compensation.

The Protect College Sports Act would not eliminate NIL opportunities such as Woods' partnership with TaylorMade. Athletes would still be free to pursue outside endorsement agreements and marketing relationships. Instead, the legislation seeks to establish a national framework for college athletics while providing additional revenue-sharing opportunities through schools, a move supporters believe would reduce uncertainty for athletes and athletic departments alike.

The bill also includes provisions aimed at protecting Olympic and non-revenue sports, a category that includes golf. Backers argue that without federal intervention, schools facing mounting financial pressure could be forced to reduce scholarships, cut roster spots or eliminate sports. The legislation would allow schools to direct additional revenue-sharing funds toward women's and Olympic sports, a measure supporters say could help preserve opportunities for future golfers.

That matters for players like Woods and the next generation of elite juniors. As NIL has transformed recruiting and athlete compensation, concerns have grown about whether smaller sports could lose ground while schools direct resources toward football and men's basketball. Supporters of the legislation contend that a more structured system could help maintain funding and scholarship opportunities across all sports.

The proposal still faces a vote in the House before it can reach President Donald Trump's desk, but its progress is another sign that the NIL era is entering a new phase.

title: US Senate passes landmark overhaul of college sports
description: The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting con
fullText:
The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.

The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act would regulate how universities pay athletes, restrict transfers and give the governing NCAA limited protection from antitrust lawsuits after years of court battles transformed the economics of college athletics.

The vote was one of the Senate's last major legislative acts before lawmakers leave Washington to campaign for the November 3 midterm elections.

The bill now goes to the House of Representatives, which is already in recess until after Election Day, leaving a narrow window for Congress to complete work before a new legislature takes office in January.

President Donald Trump's administration has endorsed the legislation, and the 80-year-old leader himself cheered the bill's passage Monday night, posting to his Truth Social platform that "it will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."

Unlike university sports in most countries, American college athletics is a vast commercial enterprise.

More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting contracts.

The legislation follows years of upheaval during which athletes won the right to profit from their names and images and, following a 2025 court settlement, universities began paying players directly.

It would establish national rules governing those payments and allow schools to spend nearly $50 million annually through revenue-sharing and other funds.

Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without sitting out a season, while agents' fees would be capped at five percent.

The bill also provides longer-term scholarship and healthcare protections and seeks to safeguard women's and Olympic sports.

Supporters argue that nationwide rules are needed to replace a patchwork of state laws and repeated litigation.

"Student athletes deserve to get paid. They deserve real protections. And high school athletes deserve a fair shot to compete," said Senator Ted Cruz, who co-sponsored the bill.

"The Protect College Sports Act delivers that while protecting women's and Olympic sports and preserving the game we love for generations to come," the Texas Republican added.

But the measure has divided Democrats and drawn opposition from racial equality activists, labor unions and the Congressional Black Caucus.

Critics say its antitrust protections give too much power back to the NCAA while limiting athletes' legal rights and leaving unresolved whether college players should ultimately be treated as employees entitled to collective bargaining.

The House could seek changes, potentially forcing another Senate vote and complicating efforts to send the legislation to Trump before the current Congress expires.

Clippers news: LA sends strong message to fans at Media Day after Kawhi Leonard scandal appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

LOS ANGELES — The LA Clippers officially kicked off their season on Monday with Media Day at Intuit Dome. It was the first step in what will be a long journey back after the NBA handed down one of the harshest punishments in sports for their role in the Kawhi Leonard salary cap circumvention scandal.

In addition to the loss of five future first round draft picks, the NBA's punishment included a one year suspension for owner Steve Ballmer and a six month suspension for President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank.

That means general manager Trent Redden has been promoted to interim President and Mark Hughes is promoted to interim general manager.

Before Media Day officially kicked off with player interviews, Redden and Clippers head coach Tyronn Lue met with members of the media and provided a lengthy opening statement with regards to the NBA's investigation.

"Obviously, this took a little longer than we had hoped. You guys deserved to hear from us before this. Our fans deserved to hear from us before this. And for that, we're sorry. We've been listening, though, not just being quiet, but listening to the thoughts, the concerns, and feeling the emotions of our fan base. They mean everything to us. Their pain through this time is real. And we feel it and we hear them, as well as our staff members who are proud to be part of this organization. We hope to fulfill our promises to them to build their trust and move forward through this time.

"The penalties we are facing are significant and we will comply with it. It will go hand in hand with our mandate to our fans, to work to build their confidence as we go through the NBA's mandates and penalties this season. Personally, Ty and I are going to miss [Lawrence Frank] and Steve [Ballmer] immensely. We wouldn't be here if it weren't for them. And they have led us through a lot of different times. It will be a challenge without them, but what they prepared us for, although this unique circumstance is new. But the opportunities they've given us, the knowledge they've taught us will lead us, and they put together a staff that can offer us behind us and help fulfill all the things that we want to this season.

"In addition, Ty and I have both been able to meet with John Gibson, our interim governor, who is a leader and a steward for us during this difficult time, not just to us in basketball operations, but also on the business side. These challenges are large, not just the penalties, but some of the injuries that we've already faced as well. This franchise often has done its best work with his back against the wall. Training camp starts tomorrow. And we've got a deep group of players that have shown competitive spirit time and again, in a coaching staff led by Ty, who we thinks the best in the NBA. We hope to represent our fans the same way we always had in dark times by coming out and fighting."

Trent Redden opens up Clippers media day with a statement apologizing to fans and saying they’re listening to everything that’s been said about them. pic.twitter.com/QXc82eZdEN

— Tomer Azarly (@TomerAzarly) September 28, 2026

The statement is primarily directed towards the fans, who have been mostly neglected throughout this entire summer after the NBA came out and handed the Clippers their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard.

Coach Tyronn Lue also added his statement on the morale of the LA Clippers franchise

"It's been difficult," Lue said. "Losing Steve and L. for this time, but I give our players a lot of credit. Since Day 1, we said we wanted everyone back the day after Labor Day, and we've had guys in the gym for two months now. Just working and trying to get better. I give our players a lot of credit for being here every single day. Everybody showed up. The leadership is great, the morale is great, even in these tough situations. That's good to see when you have your players coming in and giving everything that they have. A lot of teams don't have that."

The LA Clippers have traveled to Hawaii for training camp, where they'll be until they take on the Golden State Warriors on Sunday, October 4th.

fullText:
The Protect College Sports Act is halfway home.

U.S. senators on Monday overwhelmingly voted to pass legislation intended to bring regulation to an unruly industry — a historic moment in NCAA history but one expected after lawmakers advanced the bill through multiple procedural steps over the last week.

The bill, mainly authored by Republican Sens. Ted Cruz and Eric Schmitt and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell, garnered 77 supporting votes in the 100-member chamber — a considerable margin in such a divided Congress and a result that now sends the legislation toward the House of Representatives in an authoritative way.

"We wanted a big bipartisan vote," Cruz said earlier Monday. "We got a big bipartisan vote."

But as supportive lawmakers celebrate their thundering victory, a question continues to loom: Will the legislation pass the House?

"That bill is dead," said one Democratic House staff member.

"We have no intention to return to take up this bill before the midterm elections," said another.

Even the most ardent supporters of the legislation believe a stiff challenge awaits in the 435-member House, which historically operates in a more unpredictable manner because of its sheer size, diverse makeup and clashing cultural and geographic beliefs — even among those within the same party. Unlike the Senate's 60-vote procedural voting threshold to bypass the chamber's filibuster, House legislation only needs a simple majority for passage.

In the House, Republicans hold a four-vote margin — for now.

There are landmines that threaten to tank the bill across the landscape of the lower chamber of Congress. That starts with the elections themselves on Nov. 3.

House members are not scheduled to return until Nov. 9, after the midterm elections, where many projections have Republicans losing control of the chamber.

Cruz says he's held "extensive conversations" with House Speaker Mike Johnson and Cruz continues to believe that the House will return before the elections to take up the Act. "The House can pass this in one day," Cruz said earlier Monday.

Despite Cruz's confidence, House officials — even Johnson himself earlier this month — contend that will not happen.

Before the new Congress takes over in January, a five-week House work session (Nov. 9-Dec. 17) is scheduled, often referred to as the "lame-duck" period. The period is known for its unpredictability as outgoing lawmakers — those who did not seek re-election or lost their bid — may vote in more of an unusual manner.

If the Democrats win back the House during the midterm elections, will they vote for legislation in a chamber that, in just two months, they will control?

Either way, the fact that the House doesn't plan to return before the elections means that, in likely some way, the results will impact membership views and perhaps voting trends. It creates more unpredictability in a chamber that swims in volatility.

This is no normal bill, either.

The legislation would grant the NCAA an antitrust exemption — a rarity! — to limit athlete transfer movement (one transfer without penalty); standardize a five-year eligibility policy; more strictly regulate a new, increased player revenue-share cap; create an agent registry with a maximum 5% fee.

The bill also paves the way for Football Bowl Subdivision conferences to pool their media rights; features an anti-conference expansion section; and prevents coaches, who have left before a team's season ends, from performing duties at another university (the so-called Lane Kiffin Rule).

For years, perhaps even decades, animosity and dissension has existed between the upper (Senate) and lower chamber (House) of Congress.

That may be stronger now than ever.

"The House doesn't just take bills because they have passed the Senate," said one congressional expert who's spent years on Capitol Hill. "This is personal. Ted Cruz is holding up several House bills in the Senate."

It's personal for another reason: House lawmakers poured years and resources into a separate college sports bill, the House-authored SCORE Act, which failed to gain the necessary votes in the chamber twice last fall and again this past spring. The SCORE Act, friendlier to the NCAA and authored by Republicans, did not even garner enough Republican support.

The legislation even struggled to advance through the first step in the House's bill approval process, which is passage through the House Rules Committee, made up of Republican and Democrat lawmakers.

Many House members, comparing the two bills side by side, want the PCSA revised with components that existed within the SCORE Act, including most notably a provision that prevents college athletes from being deemed employees.

There are plenty more problematic issues for House members, such as the legislation offering athletes a pathway to private right-of-action (Republicans traditionally don't support such a concept); those against heavy government involvement in any industry; uncertain funding around historically Black colleges; and a conference expansion provision that's flustered several state delegations whose universities hope to, one day, move conferences — Florida's most of all.

Last year, the 58-member House Congressional Black Caucus — a group of left-leaning Democrats — stood against the SCORE Act. Also last year: Some of the 30-plus member House Freedom Caucus — right-wing Republicans — did the same.

This is a good example of an issue — regulating college sports — that has created divide within parties and generated strange bedfellows.

The many factions and groups in a 435-member chamber often complicate any voting process.

Already, the CBC has publicly opposed the Protect College Sports Act. Freedom Caucus members are expected to raise key concerns, including possibly wanting a limitation on foreign athletes permitted on college rosters.

Some Freedom Caucus and CBC members are on the all-powerful House Rules Committee, a group that must approve any legislation for it to reach the floor for a vote. There is a more unconventional way for legislation to reach the House floor, such as a suspension of the rules, which Speaker Johnson can call. However, a suspension bill vote must gain two-thirds majority for passage — a difficult task.

That doesn't mention House-induced revisions and amendments to the bill that would then need Senate support.

Buckle up for several more weeks of lobbying, stumping and — unfortunately — political ad campaigns.

title: Monroe County Region high school sports roundup for Saturday, Sept. 26

NEWPORT – Jefferson's boy cross country and Ida's girls took home championship trophies from the 42nd annual Jefferson Invitational.

Claire Miller of Jefferson also was a winner at Sterling State Park on Saturday, Sept. 26.

Jefferson and Grosse Ile tied for first in the boys Division 2 race with 51 points, but the title went to the home team on the fifth-runner tiebreaker rule.

Ida fourth with 102 led by Laundon Gauer, Cameron Cogan and Jude Myers finishing 11-18-19.

Fifth-place Flat Rock was led by Brayden Brodie finishing seventh.

Ida placed six girls in the top 18 to score 44 points in the girls Division 2 race, 7 better than runner-up Grosse Ile.

"The girls did really awesome," Ida coach Laurie Bayles said. "This is the point in the season where you really want to see PRs and drops."

Ida's Lana Benware was the runner-up and had plenty of help from Camilla Mommerency (7), Brynn Lusky (8), Ava Lowrie (14) and Zoey McCain (18) and Adilyn Stotz (20).

Miller won the race in 20:18.7.

"Claire Miller is my ultimate team leader for boys or girls," Ludwick said. "She is the one who makes me the absolute happiest when she does well because she just puts her head down and does the work."

Randee Mulherin was third for Jefferson. The Bears also got 15-17-23 finishes from Katelyn Steinhour, Kinsley Wilburn and Jessie Cole to take third place as a team.

Dundee was fourth with Addy Ringbloom placing sixth and 11th, respectively.

Fifth-place Flat Rock was led by Gwen Dalton (13th) and Avery Wilde (19th).

fullText:
In a recent report, Sky Sports stated that Tottenham Hotspur are keeping a keen eye on Brentford winger Kevin Schade. It has been claimed that Spurs are big admirers of the German wide player but are facing competition from Chelsea, Arsenal and Liverpool in the race to sign him next year.

Schade has made an impressive start to this Premier League campaign as he has put in a few impressive displays for the Bees in the final third. The 24-year-old has banged in three goals in six appearances for Brentford this season across various competitions.

The German sensation is currently among the most talented wide players in the Premier League. Hence, it is no surprise that Spurs are hoping to get him on board next year.

His current contract at the Gtech Community Stadium will run out in the summer of 2028, which could open the door for Tottenham to land him on the cheap at the end of this season.

AMSTERDAM, NETHERLANDS – SEPTEMBER 24: Kevin Schade of Germany runs with the ball during the UEFA Nations League 2026/27 group phase match between Netherlands and Germany at Johan Cruijff Arena on September 24, 2026 in Amsterdam, Netherlands. (Photo by Lars Baron/Getty Images)

Schade is a good dribbler with the ball at his feet and can make some driving runs with it out on the flanks. He has the eye to play some decisive passes in the final third and can shoot the ball with power from long range.

The German talent can contribute by scoring a few important goals for his team. Schade is primarily a left-winger but can also operate as a right-sided wide player or as a centre-forward if asked to do so. He is already quite familiar with the Premier League and won't take any time to adjust to life at Tottenham.

We can expect Schade to improve the quality of Spurs head coach Roberto De Zerbi's attack. He is good enough to challenge for a regular starting place at the North London club.

At 24, Schade has his best years ahead of him, which makes him a good fit for the North London club's needs in the long run. He will also help Spurs get back to challenging for a top-half finish in the Premier League over the next few years. Therefore, De Zerbi would be wise to snap him up next year.

What is Yankees’ Aaron Judge facing? Surgeon weighs in on possible return, calf re-injury risk
description: A sports surgeon details when Yankees captain Aaron Judge might be able to return from a calf strain.
fullText:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.

The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.

Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.

At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.

The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.

1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.

2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.

3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.

How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?

As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.

"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''

Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."

What can we unpack from what little we know?

NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).

"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."

Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.

"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."

Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.

If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.

"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."

Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.

"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."

The location of his calf strain is problematic.

"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."

If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.

"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."

That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.

Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon

Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:

"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.

"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."

title: 'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict
description: As Southampton manager Tonda Eckert awaits the FA hearing into his 'Spygate' misconduct conduct charge BBC sports editor Dan Roan speaks to him and club chief executive Phil Parsons on what happens next.
fullText:
More than four months since the Spygate scandal erupted, Southampton manager Tonda Eckert's wait to discover his fate for authorising an espionage campaign is almost over.

This week, a decisive Football Association hearing is set to take place, after the German coach was charged with misconduct in July.

Spying on three clubs has already cost Southampton the chance of promotion to the Premier League (worth £200m), after they were expelled from the Championship play-off final. An EFL panel also docked the club four points for this season.

As the club prepared for the latest twist in the saga, BBC Sport spoke exclusively to both Eckert and Southampton chief executive Phil Parsons, who - in his first interview on the case - insists any further punishment would be "really tough to take".

But how are the club and their coach dealing with the prospect of more turmoil? What is at stake? And why have Southampton given a permanent role to the intern who was caught spying on Middlesbrough in May?

"I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothing that prepares you for that. There just isn't."

Eckert speaks slowly and with an intense gaze when asked to reflect on being at the centre of one of the biggest controversies in English football history.

The 33-year-old apologised in June after an EFL independent disciplinary commission found he had orchestrated a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich Town, then Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.

Having insisted he was unaware it breached EFL rules, and that the spying had no impact on performances, Eckert was backed by Southampton.

His team have made an encouraging start to the new season. Without the four-point deduction, they would be fourth in the table, rather than 13th.

"We've talked a lot over the summer of how we want to go through that process of addressing everything, giving everyone the chance to put questions out that are still there, to put out what they feel and have gone through, and then also close the door and move on," he says.

"Because the reality is it's a new season. We have big ambitions as a football club, and in order to reach them, we need to move on."

That is easier said than done, with Eckert in limbo while he awaits the outcome of the FA's disciplinary process.

"I've had the chance to sit down and just talk the FA through everything that happened," he says. "And now it's up to them to make a decision. I don't really have any emotions towards that."

So does he feel the FA has listened to him during its investigation?

"That was my impression," he says. "We sat for almost four hours, so it's been quite a long conversation."

When asked whether he feels the club has been punished enough, and if a suspension for him would be excessive, Eckert chooses his words carefully.

"It's been a big, big punishment," he says. "Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports.

"And it's tough for me to say that because it concerns me. I'm judging on myself, not an outside situation. But I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly.

"I think the punishment has been very hard on the club for the last season. And to go into a new season on minus four. And the rest is not for me to decide."

Southampton owner will not sack head coach Eckert

Parsons is more forthright on whether the club has been punished enough.

"We don't know what the FA will actually hand out," he says. "It could be a long ban. It could be a short ban. It could be a suspended sentence.

"What we hope as a club is they actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account. I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history.

"This isn't just about the club, this is about people. We lose money not being in the Premier League, but [local] businesses lose money. We had to spend a huge amount on legal fees, and it really impacts the club even further. We don't want to be seen as a victim of this. We need to get on. We've had our cards dealt."

When it is put to Parsons that the EFL's punishments applied to the club - rather than Eckert himself - he says: "I think it's impossible to sanction the manager without the club getting hurt even more."

The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year, after opponents New Zealand were spied on.

Parsons insists "the Canadian case is very different" but if Eckert , who is only contracted until the end of the season, is also banned, how long would it have to be for the club to look elsewhere for a new coach?

"We don't know," he says, firmly denying having approached other coaches in case Eckert has to leave. Parsons also says the club may appeal if the ruling goes against them.

"We can't worry about something we can't control at the moment," he says. "We have to deal with it when we get there but we're hoping that they look at it sensibly."

Parsons says the club's ownership "want" to back Eckert.

"We've been through an entire transfer window when it comes to recruiting players for Tonda, and that's another challenge.

"We have to be looking at all scenarios. We've always spoken about any punishment being disproportionate...You're looking for fairness in approach. And have we had that treatment to us, from a disproportionate punishment? Well, I think a lot of people will view it that way. But do we want to sit there moaning about it? No.

"But it's going to be really tough to take if we get another punishment, on top of being thrown out of the play-offs, four points this season, and potentially more. So we're really hoping that the FA, the panel, are looking as this with a balanced view to what's already happened, because it's been really heavy."

When compared to the £10m fines that both the FA and Premier League handed Chelsea this year for making £47m in secret payments related to transfers across several seasons when they were owned by Roman Abramovich, some would agree Southampton have suffered enough.

Others however, would say the FA has little choice but to sanction Eckert.

After all, according to the EFL commission, the club employed "a particularly deplorable approach" by using junior members of staff to conduct the spying "at the direction of senior personnel".

An arbitration panel then detailed how a junior analyst intern said he felt under "extreme pressure".

Southampton's initial response to the crisis also contained "inaccuracies". Middlesbrough's head of football Kieran Scott said the club's behaviour had been "disgusting"., external

Parsons shrugs off such criticism.

And when it is put to him that many expected Southampton to sack Eckert, and had they done so they would not be facing the current uncertainty, he replies: "Yeah, but Tonda also picked up the team in around 20th place in the Championship, and without him and his team we wouldn't have been in the play-off positions, and I think that deserves a bit of loyalty.

"OK, he has made a mistake and he's paid for that dearly. This has been really tough for him as a person already. I admire how strong he's been through this process because a lot of people could have cracked, the amount of pressure he was under."

For his part, Eckert says he is "very grateful for the support of the club because that could have been very different, and I think in most cases would have been very different".

The vast majority of Southampton fans that BBC Sport spoke to also seem to fully back the manager, something he says "means everything" to him.

Another to be supported is the intern involved - Will Salt - who was recently handed a permanent role as an analyst in the club's academy.

The scandal began when a photograph was published of Salt secretly filming Boro from behind a tree at their training ground before the play-off semi-final.

"He's been through a tough time," says Parsons.

"When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with. A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club."

Asked if reintegrating Salt had been challenging, given his allegations about the way he was treated, Parsons says: "I don't think Will said he felt under pressure directly from Tonda himself. He felt under pressure in the situation. And everybody knows in a job you can feel under pressure.

"But, yeah, I think Will's managed himself really well, and he'll grow from this."

So has the club learned its lessons? Parsons insists Eckert has studied the EFL's regulations, but also argues the rules could be clearer.

"They're very grey - that's something I'll continue to raise in EFL meetings," he says.

"But look, we've done something wrong, we'll get on with it."

Moving on is not easy, though. Last week, Wrexham's owners aimed a dig at Southampton by referencing the scandal in a social media advert before the two teams met. And during matches, rival fans regularly remind the club of the scandal.

"History is history and it'll be a part of our story going forwards," says Parsons. "It's about how we react now. It's given us a real togetherness and hopefully that continues through the season because we're stronger like that anyway.

"There's a bit of siege mentality as well, right - of 'everybody's against us', so we've got to embrace it."

The Championship has now paused until next month for the international break.

For now, however, his future remains uncertain.

title: No WMU scare for Michigan football in final tuneup vs UTEP
description: Four Free Press sports writers make their Michigan football vs UTEP prediction on Saturday, Sept. 19.
fullText:
Michigan football is rolling into its final nonconference game against UTEP with a 2-0 record and feeling pretty darn good after a wild start to the 2026 college football season.

Michigan surprised people with a fantastic turnaround from Week 1 to Week 2, knocking off an Oklahoma squad that was in the top 10 after needing a Hail Mary to beat Western Michigan in the first game.

Now it's the final chance for Michigan and quarterback Bryce Underwood to show some more signs of growth and some more firepower against a UTEP squad that should be overmatched.

The Wolverines moved up five spots to No. 19 in the US LBM Coaches Poll rankings after a huge win over the Sooners at the Big House in Week 2.

So will Underwood and the Michigan offense make a statement against UTEP, or will it be another close call like Week 1 against the Broncos?

Our Free Press experts make their score predictions for Saturday's game (3:30, BTN) at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor.

While the transitive property isn't as consistent in football as it is in math, there's reason to believe U-M should roll here. Michigan beat Oklahoma, which beat UTEP 51-0 in Week 1. The Wolverines have given up one touchdown in two games against two notably better opponents. With U-M likely to have favorable field position and possess the ball frequently, it will give the offense a chance to find its form. The attack will look much better and Michigan ends the non-conference season undefeated. The pick: Michigan 41, UTEP 3.

Oklahoma beat the Miners by 51. Transitive properties should apply here. The Wolverines will take it easy and get reps for their entire roster. It should also be a chance for Bryce Underwood to work on the passing game. The pick: U-M 45. UTEP 3.

UTEP lost to Oklahoma 51-0. Michigan beat the Sooners, 17-10. If the transitive property is applied to this matchup, then the Wolverines should dominate the Miners. They will. Unlike Michigan's opener, this game will be decided long before the final second. The pick: U-M 38, UTEP 3.

This is like an NFL preseason game. The only goal is to stay healthy for the Wolverines and get to the next week. So, what should Michigan do? Put a bunch false tendency on tape. Or go so vanilla, nothing can be gleaned from it.  So, yes, Michigan will roll. Everybody will leave happy. And it won't mean a thing. The pick: U-M 45, UTEP 7.

title: Kirb Herbstreit offers flimsy defense for ESPN's decision to interview Ted Cruz on College GameDay
description: ESPN committed a bizarre broadcasting faux pas last Saturday, by giving Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) an extended platform on College GameDay to push for the passage of the so-called Protect College Sports Act (which also could be called the Screw College Players Act or, as Simms suggested, Protect the ESPN and SEC Contract Act).
fullText:
ESPN committed a bizarre broadcasting faux pas last Saturday, by giving Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) an extended platform on College GameDay to push for the passage of the so-called Protect College Sports Act (which also could be called the Screw College Players Act or, as Simms suggested, Protect the ESPN and SEC Contract Act). The story has resonated throughout the week, and it looms over Saturday's episode of College GameDay in Oxford, Mississippi.

Kirk Herbstreit, one of the College GameDay analysts, addressed the situation in comments with reporters on Friday.

"I was first really impressed," Herbstreit said, via Mississippi Today. "I've never seen a guy booed that long and be able to just power through that. You know, I don't know if he could hear what I could hear, but it was pretty — I think he was booed pretty much the entire time he spoke.

"I don't really get into politics. It's just not — I'm kind of an independent guy, right down the middle of the fairway. I'm for America, so whoever helps us as a country, I'm for. Whether it's somebody on the left, somebody on the right, so I don't really follow it. I don't know anything about his political views. I don't know what he's for or against. I care about football, my family, and my faith, and my country. Those are things I love.

"And so, I don't really pick sides, and I was surprised. I didn't know what his deal was, so him being booed, I asked people, 'Like, what's going on here?' And we had him on because they were gonna be voting this week, and maybe he could give us some insight to what's going on. That was really it. So we're not picking sides in any way at all. We just want to see the chaos that's surrounding this sport kind of be reeled in, and if this will help us get to that, then great. Now, the fact that the guy that sits right next to me, Nick Saban, was heavily involved in putting this act together, this guy loves college football more than anybody I've ever met. And so if he's happy about what this could do, then I follow his lead. But yeah, that was surprising. But, again, I don't really follow it, so I didn't really understand it."

There's a lot to unpack there. I'll keep it simple. Herbstreit is either flat-out lying or he's ridiculously naive.

How can anyone say "I love my country" while being completely detached from the issues that shape its present and future? How can any American adult not know what it means to be a Republican or to be a Democrat, and how those labels have become so inherently polarizing and conducive to negative reactions?

Beyond Herbstreit's claim that he's clueless as to why someone like Ted Cruz would be booed, Herbstreit's position that he's "right down the middle of the fairway" and that ESPN isn't "picking sides" on the issue at hand can't be reconciled with his viewpoint that the "chaos" needs to "kind of be reeled in" and that he supports anything Nick Saban recommends on the matter because Saban "loves college football more than anybody I've met."

It's entirely possible to love college football and to want to limit player pay and mobility. Which is precisely what the Screw College Players Act will do.

The word "chaos" is a matter of perspective. From the players' perspective, it's not chaotic; they have real rights and power. From the perspective of those who don't like the fact that the rabbit has the gun, it's definitely chaotic. Because the rabbit has the gun.

The best news is that folks seem to be figuring out what's going on here. The powers-that-be don't like the fact that they've lost some of their power, given the implosion of a system that was fueled by antitrust violations that collectively prevented players from getting paid. In the aftermath of the reckoning, those who don't like the new reality are shedding crocodile tears and screaming "the sky is falling" to anyone who may be able to help them implement a system that limits the new rights the players enjoy.

It's a grift. It's a scam. Herbstreit has made himself part of that scam while pretending to be neutral — and not even his dog will shield him from the criticism he now deserves.
