title: We Need to Protect College Sports from Ted Cruz
description: Elie...
fullText:
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent looks at the many ways Ted Cruz’s college-sports bill threatens athletes’ labor rights. Plus: why our mail-in voting nightmare isn’t over.

In a 7-2 ruling, the Supreme Court rejected Donald Trump’s attempts to use the US Postal Service to manipulate the upcoming midterm election. The case was on the court’s shadow docket, so the justices in the majority didn’t bother to explain themselves. Alleged attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh did offer a one-paragraph concurrence in which he argued that the Postal Service has the authority to implement Trump’s voter-suppression rules but that we are too close to the election for the rules to be changed. Justice Samuel Alito dissented, joined by Clarence Thomas. Alito argued, as he often does, that Trump should essentially be allowed to do whatever he wants to accomplish his goals.

I must point out that Thomas and Alito have the most direct interest in Republicans’ winning the midterms and maintaining control of the Senate. Their ability to retire in 2027 or 2028, under a Republican president, is directly tied to Republicans’ winning in November. I’m not exactly saying that their personal retirement planning influenced their opinions in this case, but that’s only because their extremist views of executive power happen to align perfectly with their retirement planning in this situation.

Despite their objections, this is a win. When the Supreme Court has ruled against Trump in the past, it’s usually with a wink and a nod toward how he might win the same case in the future. In this case, the court foreclosed Trump’s chance to use the Postal Service to limit mail-in voting and rig this election—and while Kavanaugh tried to throw Trump a bone for 2028, it does not appear that John Roberts or Amy Coney Barrett are interested in these particular shenanigans. The court did the right thing, and that happens rarely enough that it is worth acknowledging.

Trump, as is his wont, took the loss with the grace of a mob boss who believes the cops he’s got on the take have betrayed him. He criticized the justices he appointed to the court (Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Neil Gorsuch, who all voted to protect mail-in voting) by writing on social media, “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” and raging that the Supreme Court lacks the “courage” to “save America.” Ironically, I generally agree with Trump that the court lacks the courage to save America from him, but in this case Roberts seemed to find his inner Mike Pence and do the absolute bare minimum.

I assume Trump and his acolytes are busy planning a counterattack. Having failed to stop the ballots from being mailed, I imagine the next thing Trump will do is try to stop mailed ballots from being counted. It’s always the counting of votes that really bothers him anyway.

I expect we’ll all be back in front of the Supreme Court this November, waiting for them to tell us whether or not our votes matter.

Law professor Noah Feldman took to Instagram and TikTok to crawl all the way up Kavanaugh’s ass and offer a defense of the man more pathetic than anything we might have seen from Tobin and Squee. Feldman argued that Kavanaugh has been essentially forced to become a hardcore conservative on the Supreme Court because the left was really, really mean to him during his confirmation hearings and won’t welcome him back. Since Kavanaugh is desperate to be liked, Feldman argues, he’s had no choice but to rule with the fascist policies of the Trump administration so he can still have friends in the cafeteria or something.

I’m paraphrasing Feldman a bit, but only a bit. Here’s the direct quote from Feldman’s substack (emphasis in the original):

Justice Kavanaugh is a social person, he needs friends. But once liberals had turned against him, he really couldn’t afford to lose conservatives, because then he would have been entirely friendless—a situation not dissimilar to that experienced by Chief Justice John Roberts.

And so, as a result of the confirmation hearings, I think Kavanaugh ended up in a position where he was just forced into the conservative wing of the Court.

This read on Kavanaugh is diabolical. And I say that as a person who agrees that Kavanaugh is desperate to be liked. But to suggest that the man had no choice but to turn to fascism to find friends is one of the most persistent media lies we’ve been told throughout the Trump era. People who go to the Trump side are not forced into it. Germany did not have no choice but to turn to Nazism because France was mean to it. People have myriad options to deal with rejection, yet some of them choose evil.

Understanding that systemic factors lead people into choosing facism, racism, and authoritarianism has value, but Feldman isn’t offering an analysis of those factors. He’s not offering an analysis of why privileged white boys choose extremism. Instead, he’s offering an apologia for why poor little Brett Kavanaugh does bad things. It’s a “hurt people hurt people” type of analysis.

Except Feldman also glosses over why people were mean to Brett Kavanaugh in the first place. He allegedly tried to rape somebody! Liberals and moderates did not reject Kavanaugh because they disagreed with his jurisprudence; they rejected him because they believed he tried to sexually assault somebody and lied about it. Kavanaugh is not some abused rich boy; Kavanaugh is thought to be the abuser.

Not only is Feldman engaging in bad armchair psychotherapy; he’s also ignoring the extensive  political and professional history of the man. Kavanaugh is a dude who cut his teeth under Ken Starr. He’s always been authoritarian-curious and believed in the unitary executive theory. He’s a Christofascist extremist who is more than happy to take rights away from women and the LGBTQ community. He’s in favor of public bribery, and thinks racial profiling is no big deal. He was never going to be a “moderate.” He was never going to get within spitting distance of Sandra Day O’Connor or Anthony Kennedy, because those Republicans actually sought moderate rulings. Kavanaugh, by contrast, only ever wanted to sound moderate while forcing his extremist positions down everybody else’s throat. Which is a jurisprudential philosophy that seems to me to extend to his personal life.

Feldman’s unwillingness to deal with the issue at the heart of the Kavanaugh confirmation hearings leads to this completely disgusting conclusion: “But for Kavanaugh to moderate would require a kind of political shift in which people on the center and the left were willing to welcome him into their circles and re-engage him on intellectual and constitutional issues.”

No. No I will not reengage with this alleged attempted rapist on an intellectual and constitutional level, and fuck you for asking. Kavanaugh will never be respected by decent people (much less “liked”), and to like or respect Kavanaugh is a sign of one’s own personal indecency.

In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
The Protect College Sports Act is a bill proposed by Senator Ted Cruz aimed at regulating college sports. It’s being sold mainly as a response to upheaval caused, more or less, by colleges and universities’ finally being forced to pay student-athletes some portion of the billions of dollars they generate for their schools. The bill enjoys some bipartisan support (Washington State Democrat Maria Cantwell is a cosponsor), and major college football figures have come out in favor of it.

You don’t need to follow or care about college football to know that anything Ted Cruz is a champion of is probably a very bad thing. The Protect College Sports Act is one of the most anti-labor bills proposed by this Congress, and Democrats should be ashamed of supporting it.

I know that for a certain kind of person it is difficult to think of college football players as “labor.” But they are. And yet college football players have no ability to collectively bargain. Courts have had to order colleges to pay their athletes, and then courts have had to order colleges to let their athletes leave to go to other schools. Since the New Deal, few other labor forces have had their hands tied as much as college athletes, and the Protect College Sports Act aims, first and foremost, to take away the few labor protections that do exist. The bill places a limit on the amount of money schools can pay their athletes and restricts athletes’ ability to transfer freely between schools.

It must be noted that college football players are predominantly Black, while college football coaches are overwhelmingly white. It  must also be noted that, in most states, the head football coach for the biggest public university is the highest-paid public official in that state. The college football coach usually gets paid much more than, say, the head of the school or the governor of the state. Yet the Protect College Sports Act places no limit on how much coaches can be paid, or when coaches can leave for better opportunities (or just more money) at another school.

That alone should make Democrats revolt at this bill. But there’s another horrible thing it would do: severely harm the ability of women athletes to be paid anything at all. The bill seeks to cap the amount of money a school can spend on student athletes at $20 million. That might sound like a lot, but it’s not, especially given the revenue college sports generates. If there is a $20 million cap for the whole school, most schools will spend every available dollar on men’s college football players. Most schools will spend a million dollars on the backup quarterback than spread a million dollars around the entire women’s soccer team.

In the current uncapped market, we are seeing a lot of schools spend money on women’s sports—not nearly as much as they spend on college football, but not zero. We see schools paying women athletes, especially in soccer, softball, and volleyball. All of that money will likely go away if the Protect College Sports Act gets passed.

It will all go away until the (inevitable) Title IX lawsuit, at least. But I don’t know if the current Supreme Court will uphold Title IX in this context. And if it does, which it should, that would mean less money for the labor of the high-revenue college sports.

All of the athletes, women and men, lose under this bill, and they can’t even collectively bargain to put themselves in a better position. I get why Republicans want this bill to pass: Republicans always hate labor, and particularly hate Black or women labor getting their fair share of the revenue. But this bill should be a total nonstarter for the Democratic Party.

College sports need to be protected from Ted Cruz. How can Democrats not see that?

If you enjoyed this installment of Elie v. U.S., 

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel

title: Congress Is Trying to Rip Away College Athletes’ Hard-Earned Money
description: The Protect College Sports Act will only protect the NCAA’s billions. It deserves to go down in flames.
fullText:
If you watched the first week of college football last weekend, you saw a well-funded campaign to pass the Protect College Sports Act, or PCSA. College GameDay, ESPN's flagship pregame show, hosted Texas Senator Ted Cruz to build support for the legislation. He was largely booed throughout his appearance. Cruz was interviewed by former Indianapolis Colts punter Pat McAfee, who echoed the bill's supporters by saying that college sports were in "absolute chaos," suggesting that Congress needed to act.

Perhaps the most visible proponent of the bill is Nick Saban, who was the head football coach at the University of Alabama for most of this century. He now works as an analyst on ESPN. Saban has testified before Congress to support the bill and filmed a $10 million ad campaign with Deion Sanders, the Hall of Fame NFL player who now coaches at the University of Colorado.

"The Protect College Sports Act ends the NIL chaos in college athletics by protecting our student-athletes and teams and safeguarding women's sports and Olympic programs," he tells viewers in one version of the ad. "Join the winning team today and help protect this American tradition."

What Saban declined to mention is that the bill would "protect college sports" from the athletes who play them. The PCSA is a life raft for the NCAA, its conferences, and its schools after illegally suppressing college athletes' earning potential for decades. College athletes were finally able to pursue fair-market compensation for their services over the last few years thanks to a series of major court rulings. Now the NCAA and its allies are trying to turn back the clock to keep as much of the money that college athletes generate as possible.

The bill, like any major legislation in Congress, is the product of a thousand smaller compromises between different factions of lawmakers. There are more than a few things in the PSCA that would appeal to many college sports fans. A variety of restrictions on coaching hires and recruitment would likely appeal to those alienateed by last year's Lane Kiffen-to-LSU extravaganza, though the bill does not cap compensation for coaches or administrators. Every good thing in the PSCA is a sweetener designed to make its real purpose easier to swallow.

The PSCA's centerpiece is a harsh earnings cap for all college athletes. At minimum, those athletes could collectively receive only 22 percent of the revenue derived from their performances through their schools and conferences. There are a variety of conditions that could raise that cap for individual schools to accommodate women's sports and Olympic events, but not by much and not for everyone. This would effectively entrench a recent court settlement—more on that later—into federal law for ten years unless Congress reauthorizes it. The NFL, NHL, and NBA distribute between 45 and 50 percent of their revenue to players by comparison.

The bill also sharply limits athletes' ability to switch schools by only allowing it to happen once without penalty. Future transfers would cost athletes a year of eligibility, which would be capped at five years, outside of a few narrow exceptions—if their school eliminates a sport, for example, or a head coach is fired or hired elsewhere. To further reduce athletes' bargaining power, the PSCA would impose a strict recruiting window of between two to five weeks. This would constrain athletes' ability to shop around for the best deal, so to speak, after proving themselves.

In addition to all of this, the NCAA and its components would receive two long-sought objectives. One is preemption of state laws. By legislating on these issues, Congress would be explicitly barring state legislatures from passing their own laws to regulate compensation and other key issues for college athletes. Second, and even more importantly, the PSCA gives the NCAA immunity from federal antitrust laws when it enforces rules on compensation, transfers, broadcast rights, and more among member schools and conferences. Federal antitrust laws have been a powerful tool for college athletes to keep at least some of the wealth that they generate for themselves. With the PSCA, Congress would slam that door shut.

Arrayed against the bill are labor and civil-rights groups that have strongly criticized the PSCA for what it changes and what it preserves. In a letter to lawmakers last month, the AFL-CIO warned that the proposed law would be a major step backward for college athletes' rights. "The bill empowers the NCAA to unilaterally set rules for athletes, shielded from antitrust liability, with no suggestion that the rules ever be collectively bargained with athletes at the table," the labor organization argued.

The NAACP also criticized the bill and urged lawmakers to vote against it, arguing that it would be harmful to Black students who make up a majority of players on the most lucrative college sports. "You have coaches that have been doing this for decades now, and unfortunately, the players did not have the same rights," Derrick Johnson, the organization's president, said in an interview on ESPN earlier this week. "Now that players have rights, they're saying it's unstable. I watched college football this weekend. Every stand of every game I watched was full. People were excited. The game is as rich as it has ever been. TV revenue is up."

The bill's greatest compromise is an explicit neutrality on whether college athletes are employees or non-employees. "This title is neutral on, and does nothing to alter, employee or non-employee status for student athletes," the bill's proposed text reads. Federal laws can be vague or silent on certain matters, but I'm struggling to think of another example where Congress explicitly declined to reach a decision like this in black-letter law.

"What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation," Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy said earlier this week at an event with the PCSA's opponents. "This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world. This bill seeks to give an unprecedented antitrust exemption to an industry that is violating the law every single day."

Not every college team or sport is profitable, but college sports as a whole is a multi-billion dollar industry. ESPN, for example, paid $5.64 billion for a twelve-year deal to broadcast the College Football Playoffs in 2012 when they were first introduced. Two years ago, the network signed an extension with the NCAA and its components to broadcast the games through 2031 for $7.8 billion. This is just the playoffs, with the Big 10 and the SEC also reaching multi-billion agreements with the major broadcast networks for regular-season games. And it's not just college football: Networks now pay $1 billion a year to air the annual men's basketball March Madness tournament. Some of those networks' parent companies have lobbied, both officially and unofficially, on the bill's behalf in recent weeks.

Until recently, none of that money went to college athletes. The NCAA long championed the idea that its student-athletes should not be paid or compensated to preserve amateurism in college sports. NCAA rules allowed it to punish players, coaches, and schools who offered any sort of financial benefits to players beyond a limited number of scholarships. To that end, the association also opposed any efforts to classify players as employees, to allow them to unionize, or to accept any brand-endorsement deals from third parties.

Major American sports leagues are generally structured as cartels, where member teams work together to set costs and restrict worker employment and compensation. Federal antitrust law does not look kindly upon this sort of arrangement. If businesses in most other industries colluded to raise prices for consumers, depress employees' wages, or prevent workers from changing jobs, they would be engaging in illegal anti-competitive practices that could open them up to major legal consequences.

Every major American sports league has two features that prevent this: a collective-bargaining agreement with athletes that maintains labor peace, and an antitrust exemption that shields the league from litigation over anticompetitive practices. Major League Baseball has a judicially created exemption to antitrust laws thanks to a 1924 Supreme Court ruling. Other major leagues have partial exemptions to antitrust laws by act of Congress.

The Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, for example, allows the NFL and its teams to collectively negotiate broadcast-rights packages with the networks. In exchange for this exemption, the law also prohibits the NFL from broadcasting games on Friday and Saturday for most of the season to preserve interest in high school and college football on those respective days.

To secure congressional approval of the AFL-NFL merger in 1966, the NFL also agreed to create expansion teams in certain markets favored by key lawmakers. Two key members of congressional leadership at the time, Representative Hale Boggs and Senator Russell Long, pressured then-Commissioner Pete Rozelle to promise an expansion team in their state by threatening to kill the antitrust exemption bill required for the merger. Rozelle agreed to their terms, and the New Orleans Saints began operations that same year.

Congress, when it wants to do so, can use the promise of antitrust immunity to extract meaningful changes and reforms from sports leagues. This time, the NCAA is hoping to get everything it wants without giving up anything it wouldn't be losing anyway. It is implacably opposed to recognizing college athletes as workers, fearing that they would be obligated to the provide them with the basic workplace rights that every American receives, and it does not have a statutory or judicial exemption to federal antitrust laws, despite its past occasional claims to the contrary.

As a result, the NCAA faced a wave of federal lawsuits over player compensation over the past decade. The first and most momentous ruling came in NCAA v. O'Bannon in 2014 when Judge Claudia Wilken, a federal judge in California, ruled that the association's rules forbidding athletes from profiting from "name, image, and likeness" deals, or NIL deals, violated federal antitrust law. After O'Bannon, other groups of college athletes filed a lawsuit to challenge the NCAA's restrictions on education-related compensation.

Those cases were also consolidated under Wilken, who partially ruled in favor of the athletes. In 2021, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld her injunction against the NCAA over its restrictions. The case, NCAA v. Alston, went about as badly as it could have gone for the association. Justices from across the ideological spectrum excoriated its antitrust claims. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, raising concerns about "exploiting" college athletes, warned in a concurring opinion that other NCAA rules might face a similar fate.

Finally, in NCAA v. House, the association reached a settlement with former and then-current athletes to end multiple antitrust lawsuits, which Wilken approved last year. Among the settlement's terms was a $2.8 billion compensation fund for back payments for college athletes. It also allowed schools to pay their athletes directly for the first time, with a starting cap of around $20.5 million for each school. (Athletes had already won the right in court to accept NIL payments from third parties, including school boosters.) That cap is scheduled to last for a decade with periodic increases after each school year. The settlement forms the starting point for the PSCA, though Congress has gone well beyond it to unfairly constrain college athletes' earning and bargaining power.

Perhaps the most galling aspect of the PSCA lobbying blitz is the face of it. Nick Saban is undoubtedly the best college football head coach of the past quarter century. He was also handsomely compensated for it. The University of Alabama paid him between $3.5 and $11 million each year between 2007 and 2023. Saban was paid a fair-market value for his labor, and he was able to leverage his success into greater earnings along the way. The players he led and coached had no such opportunities while playing for him.

Even as the NCAA fought to prevent college athletes at Alabama and other schools from pursuing NIL deals, Saban was able to pursue them himself. He signed an endorsement deal with insurance giant Aflac in August 2019 that made him one of the faces of its complex advertising strategy. Had one of his players signed that same deal that year, they would have lost their eligibility to participate in NCAA sports.

Fortunately, this legislation might be one victory that even Saban can't achieve. The good news is that the PSCA might not become law in the 119th Congress. While the Senate is on course to pass its version of the bill later this month, the House adjourned on Wednesday until after the November midterm elections. Speaker Mike Johnson's decision left a host of other major legislative issues on ice until the lame-duck session this winter. If the clock runs out on the PSCA, college sports and the athletes who play them will be better off for it.

title: Real Madrid Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois Wants To Own Sports Teams, Not Just Play For Them
description: Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois spoke to Forbes contributor Sam Leveridge about NXTPLAY, an investment platform, co-founded with Gonzalo Vila.
fullText:
Reaching the elite in any walk of life is no easy task. In the case of Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, he's seeking to turn his ambition and success on the field to achievements off the field through an investment platform, NXTPLAY, which he founded early this year.

The Real Madrid and Belgium goalkeeper has spent his career being managed. Coaches set his schedule, clubs set his value, and for 20 years the job has been to stop the ball, winning the UEFA Champions League twice, not decide where the money goes, but as he edges closer to retirement, that is changing.

NXTPLAY, the investment platform he co-founded with Gonzalo Vila, now holds stakes in three soccer clubs, a lighting and fan-experience partnership with Signify, and a stake in the gaming platform PlayVault. He discussed the company's origins, his own role inside it, and what comes after playing, on the sidelines of the World Football Summit in Madrid, where he and Vila presented NXTPLAY to the industry.

Most soccer players monetize fame through sponsorship deals with brands, ambassadorial roles, or even the occasional restaurant with their name on it. Yet part of NXTPLAY's mission is to bring in more elite athletes to join the group. "Some are more interested in it, some share a vision, and sometimes you need to speak to an entourage, but often they see an opportunity to see what you are doing," Courtois told me in an interview after his panel participation at the Summit.

"Others have brand deals and are less worried about investments, but eventually doing what I do I think I will create more interest when they see that what they do is good and that they can trust me with it," he explains. "Being on LinkedIn, involved in NXTPLAY, I feel like there are more opportunities coming. They see you also as a businessman, maybe they trust me more than a usual footballer."

Rather than going down that road, Courtois has worked with Vila and NXTPLAY to build a company that takes ownership positions. It's not an entirely different proposition to what he does as a player. "One big thing is the ambition to do things well, and the work ethic," he says. "As a professional footballer, you want to do things well and grow. In some deals you can share your vision more clearly, because I've been in this world for 20 years, and in other things I can learn."

He has also worked alongside some of the sport's fiercest leaders, both on the field and on the touchline, and believes that those transferable skills have been crucial to what he can achieve in the business world. "Leadership is something important, the way to delegate and surround yourself with people who understand," he says, citing Gonzalo Vila and the wider team NXTPLAY has assembled. He credits two coaches in particular for shaping how he thinks about building that group. "Learning from people like Ancelotti and Mourinho, who are very different but very good leaders and know how to build a team, that's our goal, to build a dream team."

Of NXTPLAY's three football holdings, KRC Genk, Le Mans FC, and CD Extremadura, only one can claim to be the club that produced Courtois himself. He does not pretend the Genk investment carried the same weight as the others, having come through the ranks at the club having joined them at the age of eight.

"It was an amazing feeling," he says of signing the deal. "I owe everything to them, and the great youth academy which helped me grow into the person and goalkeeper I am today."

That academy has kept producing goalkeepers long after Courtois left it for Chelsea a decade ago. Genk has since sold Mike Penders to Chelsea, Lucca Brughmans to Liverpool, and Senne Lammens to Manchester United, a production line Courtois calls a source of pride rather than nostalgia. That is at the heart of his ambition with Genk, saying, "we want to help companies to grow and become big companies, inside of technology or media, and football teams like Genk to help them become the main players in the Belgian league, we look at Club Brugge as the team to beat with their investment, stadium expansion, but we believe we can compete".

He also revealed a personal ambition. "My dream was always to play against Genk. It's never happened," he says, recalling a near-miss in the 2012 Europa League when the draw kept his Atlético Madrid side apart from them. "A Genk versus Real Madrid Champions League game would be a dream way for me to finish my career."

NXTPLAY's portfolio so far is European, but Courtois says a long-term dream has him watching the United States market, pointing to the scale of recent franchise valuations as evidence of where sport is heading. "The size of sports teams in the U.S. is huge," he says. "You can see they keep growing, and the U.S. sports market is growing. The love I have for those sports makes a great connection. We want to dream big, but it's always a step at a time."

The platform's move into gaming, through its stake in PlayVault, reflects a similar instinct, one Courtois traces back to his own experience streaming during the pandemic. "It's huge," he says of esports' potential. "Everyone can play or follow streams on their phone, it's a way of connecting." He wants NXTPLAY's athletes integrated into the platform directly and name checks a specific ambition: joining the Formula 1 esports grid. "A thirteen or fourteen year old kid with a passion for motorsport can find friends, a place to belong, and fight for a dream. Why can't it end up being a real race car?"

Courtois is not ready to say what NXTPLAY looks like once he stops playing, only that he expects to still be busy combining his love for football and business. "I haven't decided yet," he says. Coaching a first team holds little appeal to him despite holding UEFA's A and B licenses. "I'm not sure I would want to be a coach of a first team, you would get old really fast with all the players."

He is drawn instead to development work, pointing to Genk's academy as a model. "Maybe working in the goalkeeping department at Real Madrid, establishing a top academy, developing a Thibaut Courtois instead of buying one." For now, though, that remains a future project, as he admits, "I still want to play five or six more years."

The five-year plan for NXTPLAY itself is more concrete, if still early. "We want to grow into an important investment vehicle in the world of sport and media," Courtois says, adding that raising a dedicated fund is the next step to reach new markets.

title: National high school flag football rankings: USA TODAY Sports Super 25, Week 4
description: After Central's long-standing winning streak was snapped, a new team takes over the top spot.
fullText:
After four weeks atop this list, Alabama powerhouse Central snapped its four-year, 62-game win streak with a 20-12 loss to Merced (CA) this week, leaving the top slot up for grabs, shaking up their own season and catapulting Merced into its Super 25 debut. The typical California powers have maintained their perch at the top of this week's rankings, and North Carolina's Wakefield is on the move after officially kicking off its own season.

More: Merced flag football ends Central-Phenix's historic 62-game winning streak

As more states begin to kick off their seasons this month, here are the USA TODAY Sports Super 25 national flag football rankings for Week 4:

They've finally taken the crown. The Lions land themselves on top of the Super 25 for the first time this week, following the first loss in four years for previous No. 1 Central (AL). They held on to their undefeated record through a busy, five-game week, led nearly flawlessly again by sophomore QB Kate Meier. In their 41-7 win over Santa Margarita (CA) last week, Meier threw for 288 yards and four touchdowns with zero interceptions.

The Lancers get a boost over Newport Harbor this week, holding the line to add four more victories to their tally – including one over previous No. 1 Central (AL). Senior QB Alyssa McClure threw 24-for-32 for 223 yards and three touchdowns in that victory, while sophomore Annie Hoogeveen led on the other side of the ball with seven flag pulls.

The Sailors slip behind Orange Lutheran this week on the back of too-tight victories over Huntington Beach (CA) and Carlsbad (CA) and a loss to JSerra, but they've still been in good form. Newport Harbor's squad has logged wins against Mission Hills, Carlsbad and Corona del Mar since we last spoke, and have a rematch with Huntington Beach coming up Wednesday that we'll definitely be keeping an eye on.

The biggest news of the week came when Central lost not once, but twice, ending its 62-game winning streak at the MaxPreps Flag Football Showdown. After establishing themselves as an Alabama powerhouse the past four years, claiming three-straight AHSAA Class 6A-7A state titles, the Red Devils took their talent to California to face some of the toughest teams in the nation. These losses, however, came to two of the most talented teams in the nation – Merced and Orange Lutheran. While being in the losing column is a new feeling for the Red Devils, don't get used to seeing them there, as they are still one of the most dominant teams in the country.

Willowbrook is still the reigning monarch of Illinois, and it still has yet to drop a game. Senior Kaitlyn Santos has been taking the majority of the snaps, throwing 10-for-15 for 215 yards and three touchdowns vs. Stagg this week, while Madeline Carine also made the most of her time at the helm with two passing touchdowns coming from just six throws. A lot of those balls were headed for Mckenzie Edison, who caught for 247 yards and three TDs in that game.

Not far behind Central lies another Alabama powerhouse in Moody. The Blue Devils handed Vestavia Hills its first loss of the season in a 28-7 victory to continue its undefeated streak. Junior quarterback Serenity Rutledge continues to show off her accuracy and speed, completing 17-of-21 passes for 204 yards and four touchdowns while also adding 134 yards on the ground. Moody followed that game up with another victory, blanking I3 Academy 49-0.

After a disappointing loss to Grandview last week, Mountain Vista bounced back with a crucial statement win over Legend, 33-14, to reclaim the top spot in the Colorado rankings. Junior quarterback Peyton Marr was extremely accurate, completing 28-of-36 passes for 239 yards and three touchdowns. The Golden Eagles' defense, however, might have been the key to this win. The team had four interceptions, two sacks and totaled 28 flag pulls while allowing just two scores in the victory.

Legend took its first loss of the season to Mountain Vista last week in what might have been the top game in Colorado this season. However, the Titans bounced right back with a 68-0 win over Highlands Ranch. Junior quarterback Addyson Law completed 16-of-20 passes for 186 yards and five touchdowns as 11 different receivers got their hands on the ball. Mountain Vista might have been Legend's toughest battle of the regular season, so the Titans will look to keep that their only loss.

Smith's Station made a big jump this week after a massive 54-0 win over JAG. Senior quarterback Brooke Norred had a near-perfect game, completing 19-of-20 passes for 266 yards and seven touchdowns — with six different receivers finding the endzone. The Panthers still have a number of challenging matchups on their schedule, but will look to keep Moody as its only loss of the season.

St. Charles North is on the way up. The North Stars picked up three victories to maintain their perfect record this week, with two of those coming in the form of dominant shutouts. Four different players caught touchdowns in their 33-0 victory over Oswego East, with junior star Alexzandria Richardson doubling up with an additional rushing touchdown.

Huntington Beach suffered a tough, 8-7 loss against Huntington Beach (CA) this week, buffered by wins over San Marcos (CA), McClatchy (CA) and Marina (CA). Next up is already a rematch with Newport Harbor, a great opportunity for the Oilers to move up through the California flag ecosystem if they can squeeze out the win this time.

Flag football in North Carolina is finally up and running, and Wakefield has hit the ground running. Out to a 4-0 start to their season, with three of those four being shutouts, the Wolverines are looking primed for a strong title defense run in the Tar Heel state's first officially sanctioned season.

The Chargers just keep charging. Adding two more dominant wins to their tally this week – 49-0 over Lompoc (CA) and 27-6 over Ventura (CA) – to push up to 12-2, Dos Pueblos is riding a nine-game win streak into next week and primed to keep crawling up the rankings.

The Bears storm into the Super 25 this week, fresh off a headline-making victory over Central (AL) that ended the previous four-year, 62-game winning streak. Senior Averie Steverson was all over the field against the Bobcats, logging 10 receptions for 127 yards and three touchdowns. They've strung together a pretty strong, 12-2 season so far, with the main outlier being a close loss to Los Gatos (CA) this week. We'll be eager to see if their season keeps heading in the right direction.

Dimond earned a huge 6-0 overtime win over former No. 13 South Anchorage last week, earning it a spot in this week's rankings. Sophomore quarterback Emaani Fleming has yet to throw an interception this season and has averaged 46.1 yards per game on the ground through ten games. The Lynx now remain as the only undefeated team in Alaska with just eight games left in the regular season. Later this month, however will be a crucial rematch between Dimond and South Anchorage.

The Titans remain perfect at the midpoint in the season after grabbing wins from Coronado and Fountain-Fort Carson in the past week. While they eased past Coronado 52-14, Fountain-Fort Carson caused them some trouble offensively, as they scored their lowest amount of points all season. However, a win is a win, and The Classical Academy continues to do just that.

It was a tough week for Vestavia Hills, as it earned its first two losses of the season to Moody and Oak Mountain. With Vestavia Hills' starting quarterback Eden Logan still out with a leg injury, the Rebels have struggled to find poise and momentum — especially on offense. Freshman Alana Anderegg has taken over at the helm, but the Rebels are still searching for ways to win without their star player.

Not only did South Anchorage allow its first points of the season, but it also suffered its first loss to Dimond in a battle of two undefeated teams. While the Wolverines only lost 6-0 in overtime, the offense was limited all game, totaling just 143 yards. The two teams will face off once again at the end of the month, as the Lynx will try to even the matchup.

title: University considers plans to close campus by 2030
description: The campus houses the university's library, sports and health complex, and two halls of residence.
fullText:
The University of Brighton says it is considering closing one of its three campuses from 2030 in favour of condensing its operation into two sites.

A spokesperson for the university says it hopes to move its operation from its Falmer campus to its City and Moulsecoomb sites, which it says will make it stronger and more sustainable.

No decision has yet been made to close the Falmer campus and it plans to consult on the changes, the university says.

Citing pressures on universities across the UK, it said: "We're choosing to shape our own future, building a university that is stronger, more sustainable and better connected to the needs of future students, employers, communities and partners."

Closing the Falmer campus would be supported by investment into its two other campuses, the university said.

Changes to the university could affect the university's library, currently based on the Falmer campus. About 600 students currently live in two halls of residence on the campus.

The campus also houses the university's sports and health complex, facilities for its nursing and midwifery courses, and resources for trainee teachers.

Universities across the UK say they are facing financial pressures, with the neighbouring University of Sussex looking to save £35m a year in May in proposals to cut 200 jobs.

Its vice-chancellor, Prof Sasha Roseneil, said "very difficult decisions" were needed to "address the financial sustainability crisis affecting UK higher education".

title: Senate advances the Protect College Sports Act
description: ESPN has gotten its apparent wish.
fullText:
ESPN has gotten its apparent wish. Partially, for now.

The Senate has passed the Protect College Sports Act, by a vote of 74-24. It must now clear the House of Representatives.

The vote comes three days after ESPN put Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the bill's sponsors, on its flagship college football show to advocate for the passage of the act, without a contemporaneous opposing point of view. And while Stephen A. Smith has apparently chastised me for suggesting that everyone at ESPN supports the Protect College Sports Act, I don't believe that.

It was not my intent to put everyone at ESPN in the same bucket, and I apologize if I created that impression. My point was and is that ESPN's corporate position seems to be that it supports the bill, as evidenced by the fact that two of its most prominent college football analysts (Nick Saban and Pat McAfee) have argued for its passage on GameDay without any real pushback by other panelists, by Disney's reported lobbying for the bill, and by the misguided decision to platform Cruz without offering a voice representing the other side.

Here's a thought — they could have let Smith interview Cruz.

Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) also opposes the Protect College Sports Act. I'll be interviewing him on Thursday morning, for a special edition of #PFTPM.

I'd love to chop it up with Stephen A., too. We agree on plenty of things. On the things we disagree, there's a chance that, through open and honest discourse, we'd better understand each other's points of view. The country currently needs a lot more of that.

The country does not need a federal law that "saves" college sports, in my opinion. College sports are doing just fine, and the system should be required to clean up its own mess without a federal bailout that artificially limits the compensation and freedom of the people who generate the vast majority of the revenue, while leaving unrestricted the ability of coaches to hopscotch the map in chase of their next bag of cash.

title: Bristol Rovers Boss Praises West Ham For £50m Summer Masterstroke: Can They Turn It Into Automatic Promotion?
description: West Ham United have received an endorsement from Bristol Rovers boss Steve Evans, who has praised the club’s hierarchy for keeping a squad together after relegation. Speaking on Sky Sports’ EFL c...
fullText:
West Ham United have received an endorsement from Bristol Rovers boss Steve Evans, who has praised the club's hierarchy for keeping a squad together after relegation. Speaking on Sky Sports' EFL coverage, Evans described the decision as a summer "masterstroke", with captain Jarrod Bowen at the centre of his argument.

As reported by Claret & Hugh, Evans believes the retention of players has given Nuno Espírito Santo a platform that many Championship managers would envy. West Ham sit top after seven league games, and their 6-0 win over Wrexham on 11 September strengthened that position while keeping their promotion push alive.

Evans' warning had plenty of bite. He argued that, given the quality available, finishing outside the automatic promotion places would mean Nuno had failed to meet the season's target. That puts the pressure squarely on the manager, because the board has handed him a squad built to challenge immediately rather than spend a year rebuilding.

"You have first and foremost to give credit to the owners at West Ham because they've kept a tremendous squad of players together for championship football, headed by Jarrod Bowen, who will play a pivotal part.

If Nuno looks at it at the end of the season and they're not in the top two, his objective will have failed because when you look at the squad, most managers would love to have that squad at their disposal"

Evans has a strong point, although the word "failure" needs some context. West Ham United retained Bowen after a relegation that ended their 14-year Premier League stay, and the decision removed one of the risks that usually hits relegated clubs: losing their attacking players and starting again.

LONDON, ENGLAND – SEPTEMBER 11: Jarrod Bowen of West Ham United celebrates scoring his team's first goal during the Sky Bet Championship 2026/27 match between West Ham United and Wrexham at London Stadium on September 11, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Bowen's numbers show why the choice matters. He has started all seven Championship matches, with four league goals and three assists, including a goal and assist in the 6-0 victory over Wrexham. His pace, movement and finishing give West Ham a way through packed defences, especially when matches become tight and opponents protect a point.

Claret & Hugh reported in June that Bowen was the only West Ham player without a 50% relegation wage reduction, while the club pushed to keep key players together. That decision was risky because the wages remain heavy, yet it gives Nuno a core instead of forcing him through another transfer reset.

The evidence says the squad gives Nuno an advantage, but football rarely follows a straight line across 46 matches. Injuries, suspensions, fixture swings and pressure can change the picture. Still, West Ham United have the quality, experience and attacking output to make Evans' top-two demand look reasonable rather than outrageous, and Bowen gives them the sort of match-winner most Championship rivals cannot match.

title: Behind the Last-Ditch Lobbying Battle Over the Bipartisan Senate College Sports Bill
description: An opposition coalition has formed to block the bill.
fullText:
As a final vote on the Protect College Sports Act (PCSA) draws near, lobbying efforts have gone into overdrive.

Senators are scheduled to convene on the floor on Tuesday afternoon to advance the bill to a final vote on the Senate floor. Ahead of the votes, multiple sources told FOS this week they expect the bill to get the necessary 60 votes. But lawmakers in favor of the bill face an opposition coalition that has formed to block them.

The result: a week of dueling press conferences, competing ESPN segments, and involvement from powerful labor and civil rights groups. College coaches visited Capitol Hill, while players have found themselves on both sides of the debate. Behind the scenes, private strategizing and negotiating have continued.

The PCSA, the result of years of negotiations and tens of millions of dollars in federal lobbying, would be the first college sports bill to reach a full floor vote, let alone pass in either chamber of Congress.

It would double the current revenue-sharing cap on college sports but implement stricter NIL (name, image, and likeness) rules, institute a one-time transfer portal, and codify eligibility standards. It would also codify some health and safety standards and require the richest schools to maintain women's and Olympic sports roster numbers. A second section of the bill would allow schools to pool and sell media rights, prevent a power conference super league, and forbid conferences from expanding beyond 19 teams. A third section would fund broadband service at historically Black colleges and universities.

Since the September recess, co-sponsors Sens. Ted Cruz (R., Texas), Maria Cantwell (D., Wash.), and Eric Schmitt (R., Mo.) have worked to ensure the bill gets to 60 votes, one Senate aide tells FOS.

The White House has been involved as well, beyond public statements of support from President Donald Trump. White House college sports committee members Cody Campbell (Texas Tech board chairman and booster) and Randy Levine (New York Yankees president) have been key members of the lobbying effort.

Meanwhile, a left-leaning coalition has formed against the bill. Sens. Chris Murphy (D., Conn.) has spearheaded public opposition, with Sen. Corey Booker (D., N.J.) quietly assisting. In addition, labor groups including the AFL-CIO (and its sports council, which includes 10 professional sports unions) and SEIU, as well as civil rights groups, including the NAACP, have begun using their lobbying power against the legislation. They have argued college athletes should have collective bargaining rights to establish rules, rather than Congress, and have raised civil rights issues with capping athlete pay in basketball and football.

One Democratic Senate aide tells FOS that "democratic offices are hearing serious concerns about this bill from important stakeholders," and that "opposition to the bill is growing."

An informal group of agents has also have sprung up as detractors as well, according to two sources.

To complicate matters further, bill supporters are juggling an array of stakeholders requesting revisions. Several right-leaning advocacy groups (and a few senators) said the bill could override state laws banning transgender athletes from competing in women's sports—an issue senators have fixed, sources said. No major changes have been made to other aspects of the bill, however, including the expansion provision.

One of the biggest lobbying battlegrounds this week is playing out on ESPN's airwaves.

On Saturday, Cruz sat for a nine-minute interview on College GameDay. But it backfired—both he and ESPN faced backlash for the segment. Since then, ESPN has agreed to platform a detractor: During Tuesday's 6 p.m. SportsCenter, NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson will appear to lay out his concerns with the legislation.

Also this weekend, fans saw ads lobbying for the bill funded by Campbell's organization, Saving College Sports. The commercials, part of a $10 million campaign, have run each week and have already featured Saban and Colorado Buffaloes football coach Deion Sanders. Neither Sanders nor Saban were paid to appear in these ads, FOS previously reported.

Then, on Monday, came the onslaught of press conferences.

Around midday, the labor groups, the NAACP, and college athlete advocacy organizations teamed up for a Zoom press conference criticizing the bill. Players, including Maryland women's basketball player Oluchi Okananwa, LSU women's basketball player Jada Williams, and Temple football player Jackson Pruitt, said they wanted rules and regulations in college sports just as much as coaches and administrators—but that they wanted to be involved in the negotiating process through collective bargaining.

"Athletes don't want this," Pruitt said. "And truth be told, athletes aren't fully educated on what's taking place. And they weren't vetted about this."

Players also raised concerns about loopholes in health and safety standards and prohibitions on players suing schools or governing bodies. Marty McNair, the father of late Maryland football player Jordan McNair, who died from heat stroke after a Maryland football practice in 2018, agreed with them.

Four hours later, senators held a press conference in support of the bill featuring a separate group of elite men's basketball coaches, including Arkansas' John Calipari, Gonzaga's Mark Few, and Houston's Kelvin Sampson. Executive directors of the American Football Coaches Association and National Association of Basketball Coaches were also in attendance.

Coaches said they supported the transfer limits and eligibility restrictions the bill would provide. "You can sense the desperation in everybody's voices. We really, really need help. And we need it from Congress," Few said. "This bill is the best possible thing we can do right now for college athletics."

More than a dozen college athletes joined to voice their support, mostly suggesting that the bill would protect the Olympic pipeline and preserve women's and Olympic sports opportunities.

"Athletes in Olympic sports deserve protected programs. We deserve continued education. And we deserve the chance to represent America on an Olympic world stage," Michigan rower Sophia Stylianos said. "The Protect College Sports Act preserves this Olympic pipeline and the integrity of non-revenue and Olympic sport athletes."

title: Police officer assaulted during Old Firm cup match
description: The force said a 28-year-old man was arrested in connection with the incident during the Premier Sports Cup game.
fullText:
A Police Scotland officer was assaulted during Sunday's Old Firm match at Ibrox.

The force said a 28-year-old man was arrested in connection with the incident at the Premier Sports Cup game, which Rangers won 3-0.

Officers made a total of four arrests during the quarter-final clash, including a 55-year-old man for sectarian abuse.

A spokesperson said a 25-year-old man was arrested in connection with breach of the peace, while a fourth, aged 27, was arrested in connection with threatening and abusive behaviour and resisting arrest.

McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Chief Supt Stevie Dolan said the match, which kicked off at 12:00, passed without major incident and thanked the "majority of fans" for their conduct throughout the day.

He added: "A small number of offences were detected during the course of the event.

"Behaviour such as this is never acceptable and will not be tolerated."

He added the 28-year-old and 55-year-old suspects would be reported to the procurator fiscal.

There were no away supporters at the game following a "temporary arrangement" which was reached after talks between the Glasgow clubs and the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL).

title: 'Shades of Ferguson' as Neil runs show for Rangers
description: Peter Lovenrkands believes there were shades of Barry Ferguson in Dan Neil's performance on Sunday as Rangers stormed into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals at Celtic's expense.
fullText:
There were shades of Barry Ferguson in Dan Neil's performance on Sunday as Rangers stormed into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals at Celtic's expense.

That was the verdict of Ferguson's former team-mate at Ibrox, Peter Lovenkrands, who was blown away by the former Sunderland midfielder after he scored twice in the 3-0 win.

"Dan Neil ran the show from the start," Lovenkrands said on BBC Radio Scotland.

"On the ball he never lost a pass, simple things, he was doing everything right.

"I've not seen a performance like that since Barry Ferguson in the way he controlled the midfield."

The 24-year-old deservedly put Rangers in front on 23 minutes with a crisp low finish from the edge of the box and he capped off a fine team display with another emphatic finish late on.

"He popped up with goals, not just any goals, top-class finishes," Lovenkrands added. "It was an outstanding performance."

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Neil signed a three-year deal at Ibrox in July and was immediately instilled as part of Derek McInnes' leadership group.

He once again wore the captain's armband in Lawrence Shankland's absence and rose to the occasion of his first Old Firm derby, excelling in the middle of the park alongside Nicolas Raskin and James Penrice, who inverted from left-back.

"Dan is going to get highlighted for his goals - two different types of finishes - but we knew we could occupy that space on the edge of the box if we attacked properly," manager McInnes said.

"You still need people to step up and show their quality and Dan did that. His performance was really strong as well, as was Nico and wee James in there.

"The three of them were terrific and it played a big part in us getting some sort of ascendancy in the game."

Neil has grown in stature in recent weeks, but this was his finest performance in a Rangers shirt to date, getting the better of proven performers Callum McGregor and Benjamin Nygren.

At one point, Neil spun McGregor and left the Celtic captain in his wake. It was reflective of Rangers' dominance throughout the 90 minutes and Neil's own excellent showing.

"It was a great team performance," Neil told Premier Sports. "We fully deserved the victory out there.

"In the last few games we've done well without the ball. Today we wanted to use the crowd and get after them - the lads executed it perfectly."

Neil was also quick to praise McInnes' pre-match team talk and how well prepared Rangers were for such a big game.

"We all believed in the plan," he said. "The gaffer is good before games and he made sure we were ready to run through brick walls.

"That togetherness and cohesion has really come on recently."

The teams meet again next Sunday in the Scottish Premiership, with Celtic hosting Ferencvaros on Thursday in the Europa League before Rangers travel to Celtic Park.

And McInnes is delighted by the "togetherness" his team is showing before another huge game.

"It's up to us to keep reinforcing the message that when you play at Rangers there's another big game round the corner and that's what we've got next Sunday," McInnes said.

"I love the togetherness, I need to have this team who cares for each other, has love for each other. When things aren't going well you sometimes see the true strength. We've had some soul searching and tough times the past few weeks.

"It gives so much encouragement to the club, fans, the board as to what we're capable of."

title: Did O'Neill get team selection wrong in Old Firm defeat?
description: After a meek Premier Sports Cup exit at the hands of rivals Rangers, did Celtic boss Martin O'Neill get his team selection wrong?
fullText:
When Sebastian Tounekti's name appeared on the Celtic teamsheet for Sunday's Premier Sports Cup quarter-final, the collective groan from supporters could have drowned out the 50,000 strong Ibrox crowd.

With Yang Hyun-jun away on international duty, Tounekti made just his second start of the season in Wednesday's 1-0 win over St Johnstone, with former Hoops goalkeeper Pat Bonner describing his first-half performance in Perth as "awful".

The Tunisia winger lost possession 23 times against Simo Valakari's side - only opposition keeper Toby Steward coughed up possession more.

Tounekti toiled again at Ibrox up against Rangers right-back Dujon Sterling, so much so that he was hooked at half-time and replaced by Egypt international Haissem Hassan, who joined Celtic from Real Oviedo this summer in a deal reportedly worth up to £9m.

The substitution made little difference as Celtic slumped to a 3-0 defeat, having been one down at the break.

"That was a question, should Tounekti start or not?" Bonner said.

"O'Neill went with him but I think I think he now realises that maybe he's not the player that's going to be dominant in this team.

"Sterling absolutely dominated him, and Sterling was playing almost like a third centre-half.

"Out of all of the wingers we've seen, I think Hassan should have started. He's maybe not 100 per cent match fit but you pay big money for these guys they have to perform."

'McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker'

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Tounekti's spot in Celtic's front three was not the only attacking quandary for O'Neill going into the game.

Camilo Duran had excelled through the middle while Kasper Hogh - another big-money summer signing - was out injured.

But with Hogh fit again, the Dane started at McDiarmid Park and led the line again at Ibrox, with Duran moved out wide.

Both struggled to make an impact and former Rangers man Andy Halliday was scathing in his assessment of Hogh's performance.

"Kasper Hogh has blown hot and cold for Celtic so far, but he was absolutely freezing today," Halliday said on Premier Sports.

"On the ball, off the ball - no desire, no willingness to get back and defend for his team."

After Hogh was brought off on 64 minutes, Duran was deployed through the middle, only to be substituted himself 13 minutes later for Shim Mheuka.

O'Neill also opted to break up the centre-back pairing of Cameron Carter-Vickers and Auston Trusty that had started seven of Celtic's nine games this season. Kieran Tierney returned at left-back and Liam Scales shifted inside to partner Carter-Vickers.

On-loan Wolves goalkeeper Sam Johstone, who also started at St Johnstone, was perhaps a surprise inclusion given Viljami Sinisalo has kept four clean sheets in his eight appearances this season.

Despite some sharp saves in Perth, the 33-year-old looked rusty at Ibrox, maybe unsurprising given it was just his second competitive appearance since March.

Rangers striker Kevin Kelsy should have scored when Johnstone's clearance went straight to him early on and Kim Min-Su had an effort cleared off the line by Scales after the four-time England international palmed a cross into his path.

Johnstone spent the rest of the game being goaded by Rangers supporters every time he was on the ball.

"If you've been beaten in a game you always think about selection," manager O'Neill said post-match.

"I'll think about my own part in proceedings first of all and then we'll see. I wanted people to experience this atmosphere and they certainly did that today."

Gordy: Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney got team selection and formation totally wrong. It was obvious Rangers would overload the midfield and fight for the second ball, physically and mentally we were not up to the task. Colby Donovan, Mika Baur and especially Sebastian Tounekti were not up to the standard needed to play for us.

Moe: Team selection was wrong, Viljami Sinisalo should have played he had the experience already.

Phillip: Worst performance in five years, a mess from the get go starting with leaving Hassan out. Johnstone a disaster in goal, Sinisalo needs to go back in. A good look in the mirror needed and midfield signings in January.

Willie: Shocking team selection from the start.

Biggar: Martin O'Neill got two big team selection decisions wrong. Tounekti shouldn't be anywhere near the Celtic first team. Hassan should've started on the right, with Duran on the left. Sinisalo should've been back in goal, very harsh on him to lose his starting place.

title: Rangers 3-0 Celtic – “On the day, just second best,” Martin O’Neill
description: Martin O’Neill spoke to the media at Ibrox this afternoon after Celtic exited the Premier Sports Cup at the quarter finals stage following a 3-0 mauling from the Rangers…13th September 2026; Ibrox...
fullText:
13th September 2026; Ibrox, Scottish League Cup Football, Rangers versus Celtic; Dan Neil of Rangers shoots and scores in the 22nd minute to make it 1-0. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

The Celtic performance was absolutely pathetic with only young Colby Donovan worthy of a passmark. Here's everything that a shell-shocked Celtic manager had to say about today's shambolic Celtic performance….

Q: Martin, what went wrong for your team today?

Martin O'Neill: "We were well beaten in the end. I thought the first half we didn't capitalise, we had a couple of really decent chances when we'd broken their press. But on the day, just second best."

13th September 2026; Ibrox. Scottish League Cup Football, Rangers versus Celtic; Rangers fans display. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

Q: What would you put that down to, Martin?

Martin O'Neill: "I think there has to be a realisation of how big this game is. It's so important to the fans, so important to everybody. It's still one of the great fixtures, as mentioned, in European football, if not the world. And people have got to know that. That's the point. We'll have to try and learn from it. We play next Sunday, we've got a midweek game. But really we have to. I think, hopefully, it's a wake-up call. I have to look at myself for a start, then I look at the team. We were second best."

Martin O'Neill at Ibrox. Premier Sports Cup quarter final. 13 September 2026. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

Q: Did that surprise you, Martin? You said it was a wake-up call.

Martin O'Neill:  "I think it is. You can go on, you can win some games, which we've been doing domestically and it's been fine. We've found a way to win a couple of matches which were difficult for us. We were beaten today. Did Rangers surprise me? No. I think they're strong. I think they're physically strong. So it'll be a big test for us next Sunday again, in every aspect."

Q: Martin, you said that Rangers didn't surprise you in terms of their commitment and effort levels, but were you surprised that they went with three at the back? Or do you think it was difficult for Celtic to deal with that?

Martin O'Neill:  "Not necessarily. I think you have to be able to deal with it. You deal with any sort of permutation that the opposition put in front of you. That's their prerogative, to do exactly that. I'm not so sure it's always to do with systems. Sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. But if you do misplace a lot of passes, when you have comfortable possession, I don't think that's got to do with the systems, myself. I think, we did misplace a lot of passes today when we were comfortable and choosing the wrong option when we were on the counter-attack."

13th September 2026; Ibrox; Scottish League Cup Football, Rangers versus Celtic; Camilo Duran of Celtic. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

Q: Is that why you were unable to create such few opportunities?

Martin O'Neill:  "That's true. We didn't do. That's a bit of a surprise to me. The one thing that I felt, and I think I've been saying to you for weeks, certainly domestically, we look as if we can create. So it didn't materialise today. So we have to try and find out the reasons why. Just at this minute, I'm naturally disappointed, really disappointed about it. But we've got to gather ourselves together because the games are coming thick and fast for us."

Q: Martin, you made one change at the break. Were you tempted to make more, especially a couple of boys on yellow cards?

Martin O'Neill: "It could have changed. Me personally, I think young Colby has come out of this with great credit. I think he's an absolute warrior. Sometimes we misplace passes, but he's got a big heart. I think we can all learn from that. And because of the size of his heart, he was booked in the first half, but he kept going right to the end. He was booked against St Mirren after about eight or nine minutes, still kept going. In terms of heart and desire, he's been a big plus for us."

Olwethu Makhanya of Rangers is challenged by Benjamin Nygren of Celtic during the Premier Sports Cup Quarter Final match between Rangers and Celtic at Ibrox Stadium on September 13, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

Q: Martin, obviously there are no away fans on the ground today. Did that play any part? Do you think maybe some of your team are overawed by the occasion?

Martin O'Neill: "Well, a lot of boys have, you know, Kieran Tierney and Callum, people like this here and James Forrest, they've all won here when there's been big crowds. And I think they've won. Was there anybody here when Covid set in? No? So they've played here before, so that I don't know. But certainly for some of the younger and the newer lads, it's an experience that I don't think they'll forget."

13th September 2026; Ibrox, Scottish League Cup, Rangers versus Celtic; Sam Johnstone of Celtic comes off the team bus. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

Q: Martin, Sam Johnstone wasn't the only Celtic player that found it difficult today but why did you opt for him ?

Martin O'Neill: "I want people to experience these games, because what other way am I going to learn about what people can or cannot do? What I don't want to do is just put people in so that I can learn something from it. The main object is obviously to try and win, and it's a fine balancing act from me.'

Q: Martin, is it a bad day at the office, or are you more concerned about the structural problems with the team at the moment?

Martin O'Neill: "Structural in what sense?

Q: Off the ball, losing possession?

Martin O'Neill: "Yes, I absolutely agree with you. I think we can do much, much better than that. I think we can get the ball back a bit more quickly than we certainly did today, and start getting back to dominating. So we'll see what next Sunday brings. In normal circumstances, I wouldn't mind just a full week to look at a few things and maybe work on a couple of things. But yes, we had players today who were below par, and well below par, and that's not a great mix."

13th September 2026; Ibrox, Scottish League Cup Football, Rangers versus Celtic; Benjamin Nygren of Celtic and Sebastian Tounekti of Celtic. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

Q: What was behind the decision to start with Sebastian Tounekti on the left? What was your thinking there?

Martin O'Neill: "Young Hassan had an overnight problem, and he didn't get much sleep in all honesty, so it was just a matter of not starting him because of that. That's the reason, really."

Q: Do you expect a bit more from your new arrivals in some of this kind of game? Is that a bit of a culture shock?

Martin O'Neill: "I hope it is. I hope it is, absolutely. I'm sure it will be. It was a culture shock for me 26 years ago when I came here, we got smashed 5-1."

Martin O'Neill, Manager of Celtic, arrives at the stadium before the Premier Sports Cup Quarter Final match between Rangers and Celtic at Ibrox Stadium on September 13, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

Q: Martin, are you happy your next domestic fixture is against Rangers?

Martin O'Neill: "That would be good, yes. I'm looking forward to that I'm looking forward to our crowd making the same sort of noise as the Ibrox crowd made today."

title: Rams Defensive Coordinator Under Fire After Disappointing Start
description: The Los Angeles Rams were massively disappointing on both ends of the field, culminating in a 27-7 loss to the San Fransico 49ers. The post Rams Defensive Coordinator Under Fire After Disappointing Start appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Rams were massively disappointing on both ends of the field, culminating in a 27-7 loss to the San Fransico 49ers.

However, given all of the additions to the defense, that was the side with the higher expectations.

Aaron Donald returned, albeit not for Week 1, while the best defensive player in the sport, Myles Garrett, was added via trade, along with two good cornerbacks in Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie.

In 2025, this unit was already one of the better groups in the league, and with so many upgrades, it was expected to be a super unit.

The Rams allowed 27 points and had only a 5.6% pressure rate, dwarfed by the 49ers' 27.6% rate. The Niners totaled 379 yards and 5.9 yards per play as well.

On third down, SF converted seven of 12 scenarios. The Rams allowed more explosive plays, and they had no answers in the run game.

After the Rams' loss, ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky said the defense was a bigger concern than the offense, specifically calling out Los Angeles defensive coordinator Chris Shula.

"I am very concerned about that defense, and I'm very concerned about their defensive coordinator," Orlovsky said on ESPN's "Get Up!" 

"The last four games that we have watched this defense on the field with all kinds of talent, they have stunk. Bryce Young lit them up. Caleb Williams lit them up. Sam Darnold lit them up. Brock Purdy lit them up."

While Orlovsky is right that the Rams have disappointed in some marquee games defensively, this season is only one game old, and much more is to come from Shula.

The team stayed in heavy zone coverage rather than mixing in much man, which let the 49ers gash them.

The defensive scheme looked quite vanilla for the Rams overall, and they are known for hiding things they'll do throughout the season early on.

All eyes will be on what adjustments they make once Donald enters the mix and Donald gets healthy.

fullText:
Senator Ted Cruz sent a dire warning if Congress does not pass the Protect College Sports Act. In about five years, in Cruz's estimation, football and other sports will be in an unrecognizable state.

The biggest things for Cruz are the transfer rules and a hard out on eligibility for college athletes. You get one free transfer and five years of eligibility in total, which ends regardless of how many years used once you turn the age of 24. Keeping that in place, along with an even playing field when it comes to NIL, this is the best solution for football, basketball, wone's sports and other Olympic sports, per Cruz.

"There are no rules, and the situation with the transfer portal, where kids go and transfer two, three, four, five times, it's terrible for the game. It's terrible for the players. It's terrible for the schools, and it's terrible for the families," Cruz said on College GameDay. "And so the reason Congress is acting is because Congress created this problem. It was the federal antitrust laws that were used to bring the lawsuits that struck down all the rules, and so the Protect College Sports Act is bipartisan legislation that's very simple.

"It brings order to chaos. It protects the students, protects the student's ability to be compensated to receive name, image, and likeness compensation, I think that's only fair. It's only right."

Cruz is all about NIL and athletes getting compensated what they're worth. However, that's the key phrase. What they're worth and that has to do with revenue sharing and essentially the limitation of a blank checkbook.

"They're producing enormous value with an enormous skill, but it also puts reasonable rules in place," Cruz said. "So, for example, every player gets one free (transfer), not three or five, one (transfer). It puts an eligibility rule that every player has five years of eligibility, not six, seven, eight; five. And it puts a hard end on that at age 24. It lets the schools compete, and it also slows down what we've got right now (which) is a spiral of cost that is bankrupting almost every college program, most college athletic programs.

"They're losing 10s of millions of dollars, and as a result, they're canceling women's programs. They're canceling non-revenue sports. They're canceling Olympic sports. Within three to five years, we're going to see 40 to 50 schools that have competitive football programs, and everyone else goes under. That would be a tragedy."

College sports are important to Cruz and the fabric of the country, as the senator said. While football is the headlining sport in the Protect College Sports Act, everybody will be affected, hopefully in a positive way, with the bill.

"And so I think the reason Congress is going to happen is because college sports is too precious," Cruz said. "We've got to make sure this remains an avenue for opportunity for millions of kids, and we've got to make sure it remains not just football, but also all of women's sports, all of all of the non-revenue sports, all of the Olympic sports. This bill is designed to do all that."
