title: 49ers insider weighs in on possibility 49ers are sold by Jed York
description: NBC Sports Bay Area's Matt Maiocco's doesn't think Jed York's arrest will change the way he views the ownership of the 49ers.
fullText:
The fallout from owner Jed York's arrest continues to hang over the San Francisco 49ers, but NBC Sports Bay Area's Matt Maiocco doesn't believe it will cost the York family the franchise.

York was charged with two misdemeanors — disorderly conduct and possession of criminal tools — after responding to an undercover ad on what was described as a known prostitution website. He received a two-day jail sentence and a $1,150 fine. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell confirmed at the league's preseason owners' meeting that the incident is being reviewed under the personal conduct policy. York did not attend the meeting, a decision that wasn't surprising given how recent the arrest was.

Speaking on KNBR, Maiocco addressed the inevitable speculation about a forced sale directly, pointing to how deliberately the York family structured its ownership just two years ago.

"I can't see that. Jed bought equity from his mom in order to become the principal owner. Yes, the 49ers raised a lot of money by selling off around 9.7% of the organization, but when they transferred ownership officially over to Jed as the principal owner, the idea was this was a move made to ensure that it remained in the family," Maiocco said. "I would imagine the long-term plan is for Jed to hand it over to one of his sons or keep it in the family. I don't think this [arrest] will impact that. I think that there will be some discipline by commissioner Roger Goodell. I think it can happen sooner rather than later because the legal process has run its course. I would expect a fine and even a suspension, where he has to stay away from the team for a certain amount of time."

York became the 49ers' principal owner in March 2024, purchasing additional equity from his family specifically to formalize what had effectively been his role since taking over as CEO in 2010. At the time, York did frame the move as a long-term succession plan, saying it was "reflective of how we've operated" and intended to keep the team "in our family for generations to come." His mother, Denise DeBartolo York, and father, Dr. John York, remained co-chairs.

Maiocco acknowledged the situation is embarrassing for the organization and could become a talking point if the 49ers stumble out of the gate, but he drew a comparison to another franchise that weathered owner controversy without a sale: the New England Patriots under Robert Kraft.

"Nobody was talking about that with Robert Kraft," Maiocco said, "and I think it'll blow over, but it will always be kind of in the back of people's minds."

title: Today in sports history, September 21
description: Today in sports history, September 21
fullText:
Today is Sept. 21. On this date in:

1892: John Clarkson of the Cleveland Spiders defeated Pittsburgh 3-2 to become the fifth pitcher in major league history to reach 300 career victories.

1896: Connie Mack announced he would leave Pittsburgh to manage Milwaukee in the Western League, a career move that preceded his legendary tenure as an owner and executive with the Athletics.

1933: The Washington Senators defeated the St. Louis Browns 2-1 to clinch the American League pennant.

1934: St. Louis Cardinals rookie Paul "Daffy" Dean pitched a no-hitter in a 3-0 victory over the Brooklyn Dodgers, completing a doubleheader sweep after his brother Dizzy Dean threw a three-hit shutout in the opener.

1955: Rocky Marciano recovered from a second-round knockdown and stopped Archie Moore in the ninth round at Yankee Stadium to retain the heavyweight championship. Marciano retired the following year with a 49-0 record.

1961: The Minnesota Twins defeated the Washington Senators 6-3 in the final major league game at Griffith Stadium in Washington.

1963: Pittsburgh Pirates coach Gene Baker became the first Black person to take charge of a major league team when he managed the final two innings after manager Danny Murtaugh and coach Frank Oceak were ejected against the Los Angeles Dodgers.

1969: New York Jets punter Steve O'Neal launched a 98-yard punt against the Denver Broncos, setting an NFL record that still stands.

1970: The Cleveland Browns defeated the New York Jets 31-21 in the inaugural "Monday Night Football" regular-season telecast on ABC.

1971: American League owners approved the relocation of the Washington Senators to Arlington, Texas, clearing the way for the franchise that became the Texas Rangers.

1978: San Diego Padres pitcher Gaylord Perry defeated the San Francisco Giants 5-1 for his 20th victory, reaching the mark for the fifth time in his career.

1981: Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Steve Carlton struck out 12 Montreal Expos and surpassed Bob Gibson as the National League's career strikeout leader.

1982: NFL players began a strike that suspended the season for 57 days and reduced each team's schedule from 16 games to nine.

1985: Michael Spinks defeated Larry Holmes by unanimous decision in Las Vegas to capture the heavyweight championship and end Holmes' undefeated reign.

1990: Oakland's Bob Welch became the first major league pitcher in 12 years to reach 25 victories in a season.

2001: In the first major sporting event in New York after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Mike Piazza hit a dramatic eighth-inning home run to lift the Mets past the Atlanta Braves 3-2 at Shea Stadium.

2008: The New York Yankees defeated the Baltimore Orioles 7-3 in the final game at the original Yankee Stadium, which had opened in 1923.

2008: The United States defeated Europe 16½-11½ at Valhalla Golf Club to win the Ryder Cup and snap a streak of three consecutive European victories.

2014: Lewis Hamilton won the Singapore Grand Prix and took the Formula One championship lead while equaling Juan Manuel Fangio's mark of eight Grand Prix victories for Mercedes.

2019: Manchester City defeated Watford 8-0 for the largest top-flight victory in club history and became the first Premier League team to lead 5-0 after 18 minutes.

2024: The Chicago White Sox lost their 119th game, tying the 2003 Detroit Tigers' American League record for losses in a season.

title: Tony Romo receives 3 new citations following OWI arrest in Milwaukee
description: Romo is due in court on Sept. 21. It's unclear if he'll call games for CBS Sports again.
fullText:
Tony Romo has received three new citations stemming from his arrest in Milwaukee on suspicion of operating a vehicle while intoxicated, according to the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel.

According to online court records, the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and current CBS Sports analyst was cited for first-offense operating while intoxicated, unsafe passing on the right side and possessing open intoxicants in his vehicle. Romo had already received a citation on July 27 for refusing to take an intoxication test after his arrest.

Romo is reportedly due in court for all four citations on Sept. 21.

His camp also released a new statement to the Journal-Sentinel:

"Tony accepts full responsibility for his actions and has taken proactive steps to ensure that this isolated civil matter is properly resolved. We are working with local authorities to bring this matter to a close and we are communicating with CBS about next steps."

Romo was arrested on July 23 after being pulled over on a Milwaukee highway and performing poorly on a field sobriety test, according to police.

In addition to legal repercussions, Romo was soon placed on indefinite leave by CBS Sports. His future with the network remains uncertain, with company president David Berson declining to provide a timetable for a final decision while speaking with reporters earlier this month.

Romo was once the darling of NFL media and CBS paid him like it with a record-shattering 10-year, $180 million contract in 2020. His luster had worn off considerably even before the arrest, with his meandering and casual commentary style wearing thin for many fans.

So it might not be a surprise if CBS uses the arrest to get out of that contract and cut Romo loose. The Athletic noted his contract contains a morals clause that could allow CBS to void the deal if he embarrasses the company.

In the meantime, CBS is set to open the season with J.J. Watt working opposite Jim Nantz in its No. 1 booth.

title: Olympic hero Alysa Liu to sit out figure skating season before 2027 return
description: Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.  “I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve,” Liu wrote.  Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her “overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything”.
fullText:
Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.

The 21-year-old American announced her decision on social media, saying she wanted time to "recalibrate" and develop her skating away from the demands of competition.

"I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote. "It's important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth."

Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything".

"I really want to improve my skating, and I wanted to take the time to do that for myself and just to evolve," she said. "And then I'll be back after that is done."

The decision represents another unconventional turn in a career that has carried Liu from child prodigy to burnout, retirement and an unlikely return as world and Olympic champion.

Liu became the youngest ever US women's champion aged 13, when her 4ft 6in frame left her too short to reach the top of the podium without help from the other medalists. But the relentless training and attention that accompanied her rapid ascent gradually drained her enthusiasm for the sport.

She retired at 16, only months after finishing sixth in her Olympic debut at the 2022 Beijing Games, and later described how comprehensively she had come to reject the life built around her skating.

"I really hated skating when I quit," Liu said in the run-up to the Milano Cortina Olympics. "I didn't care about competitions. I didn't care about places. I didn't care about skaters. I didn't care about my programs. I just wanted to get away."

Liu enrolled at UCLA, studied psychology and went hiking in the Himalayas with friends while discovering an identity beyond the rink. Her desire to skate returned unexpectedly during a ski trip to Lake Tahoe, where gliding down the mountain rekindled her love of movement.

She began skating once a week at public sessions in El Segundo, California, and found that the difficult jumps that had propelled her childhood rise had not entirely deserted her. Liu eventually decided to mount a comeback, but only with greater control over her career, including her music, costumes, diet and training schedule.

The results would no longer define the experience, she insisted. Her initial ambition was simply to make another Olympic team and use the sport as a form of self-expression.

That approach carried Liu to a surprise world championship in 2025, making her the first American woman to win the title since Kimmie Meissner in 2006. In February, she landed seven clean triple jumps to rise from third place after the short program and win the Olympic women's singles title in Milan.

The West Oakland native became the first American woman to claim the event since Sarah Hughes in 2002. She also won gold in the Olympic team competition.

"Really the only word that comes to mind when I think about my entire journey is grateful," Liu told NBC Sports. "I think the reason why it's been so fun is because I have my own agency. I really like to skate, and so that's why I skate."

Liu said she assessed her emotional and physical state earlier this summer and concluded that stepping away was the right choice. DiGuglielmo and Scali supported the decision.

"Logically and emotionally and physically, this just makes the most sense," she told NBC Sports. "I will miss seeing the international competitors at all the international competitions, but there will be more, so it's fine."

A rush of opportunities followed Liu's Olympic victory. Nearly 5,000 people turned out for a homecoming celebration in her honor, where Oakland mayor Barbara Lee presented her with a key to the city. She withdrew from the world championships in March, performed alongside her Olympic teammates on the Stars on Ice tour, attended Louis Vuitton's Paris Fashion Week show and wore the label to the Met Gala.

Liu had been scheduled to compete at Skate America from 13-15 November in Everett, Washington.
